articles.description:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 1: Touch Grass
🌿 TrailMate AI — Your AI-powered outdoor activity planner
TrailMate AI helps people spend less time staring at screens and more time exploring the outdoors. Instead of endlessly scrolling for things to do, users can generate personalized outdoor activity plans based on their starting location, available time, preferred activity pace, and favorite scenery.
Whether you have just 20 minutes for a short walk or 90 minutes for a nature adventure, TrailMate AI suggests activities, provides a simple itinerary, recommends what to bring, and includes basic outdoor safety reminders.
The project is designed for students, busy professionals, travelers, and anyone who wants to make getting outside easier.
The main idea is simple: use AI to help people leave their screens, not spend more time on them.
🌐 Live Demo: [Not Ready Yet]
📸 Screenshots:



The demo currently includes a sample-planning mode, so users can explore the experience without configuring an AI model.
💻 GitHub Repository: [https://github.com/antonluckshman/TrailMate-AI]
TrailMate AI is built with React and Vite. The source code includes the user interface, activity-planning logic, sample plans, and optional local AI integration.
Feel free to explore the code, suggest improvements, report issues, or contribute new outdoor activities and planning features!
I built TrailMate AI using React, Vite, and open-source AI models that can run locally.
The application has two planning modes:
Demo mode: Generates sample outdoor plans immediately, allowing users to try the application without setting up an AI model.
Local AI mode: Can connect to Ollama to run a supported open-weight language model locally, such as Llama 3.2 or Qwen2.5.
Users choose their starting location, available time, preferred pace, and scenery. The application uses those preferences to generate an outdoor activity plan with suggested activities, a checklist, and safety reminders.
I wanted to make the project accessible to people who don't have access to paid AI APIs. By supporting local inference, TrailMate AI provides a path toward experimenting with AI without requiring a paid model API key.
The current version is an MVP. Its plans are suggestions, not verified hiking routes or live recommendations based on weather, trail conditions, or real-time maps.
Open innovation makes it possible for developers to experiment, learn, and build useful applications without depending entirely on proprietary platforms.
For TrailMate AI, open-weight models and local inference offer several advantages:
Accessibility: Developers and users can experiment without necessarily paying for a commercial AI API.
Privacy and control: With a properly configured local setup, prompts can be processed on the user's machine rather than sent to a hosted AI provider.
Flexibility: Different supported models can be tested and compared for activity planning.
Community collaboration: Other developers can contribute new activity types, improve prompts, add local outdoor knowledge, and extend the application.
Learning by building: Open tools make it easier to explore how AI fits into a complete application, from the user interface to model inference.
A closed API could also generate outdoor plans, but open-weight models give developers more flexibility over where inference happens and which model they choose. They also make experimentation more accessible.
I believe open innovation is especially valuable when building small projects: it lowers barriers to experimentation and gives the community a starting point that others can adapt to their own needs and locations.

articles.title: Auditable Fintech Access by Polling SMS OTP Delivery Status Without Webhooks
articles.description:
Short answer: use bounded polling only to improve the login screen, never to decide whether an OTP is valid. The least complex defensible design records one immutable send attempt, polls a provider-neutral status adapter for a short deadline, and writes every observed transition to an audit log. Verification remains a separate, atomic operation. A terminal invalid-recipient result suppresses later sends; an unknown result ends the poll without pretending that delivery succeeded or failed.
The bill is made of message attempts, status lookups, stored evidence, and operational review. For a symbolic workload of N OTP sends, p polls per send, and r retained status rows, the dominant variable term is visible without a price sheet: polling creates N * p lookups, while evidence storage creates roughly N * r rows. A policy of six checks therefore creates up to six status reads per send. Reducing six checks to three halves that lookup count; shortening retention does not. Settle that arithmetic before arguing about databases.
This separation also fits the security boundary described by the OWASP Forgot Password Cheat Sheet: codes should be generated securely, linked to an individual user, invalidated after use, and protected by rate limiting. Delivery state is useful evidence and useful UX input. It is not proof that the person entering a code is entitled to the account.
It means a bounded sequence of stale snapshots. The first lookup may still report an accepted or queued state after the handset has received the message; a later lookup may expose a terminal failure. No polling interval removes that epistemic limit. The login page should say that a code was sent, offer a controlled new attempt after a server-defined delay, and avoid promises such as "delivered" unless the adapter has mapped a terminal delivery state while preserving its source evidence.
For an illustrative policy, poll after 1, 2, 4, 8, 12, and 18 seconds, then stop at 45 seconds. These are design parameters, not carrier guarantees. Add per-attempt jitter so a traffic spike does not produce synchronized status traffic, and cancel outstanding checks when a terminal state appears. The short deadline contains load and latency; the widening gaps spend fewer reads on states unlikely to change immediately.
The awkward case matters most: the poll deadline expires while the OTP is still valid. Keep those clocks independent. Expiring observation must not expire authentication, and an authentication timeout must not rewrite the delivery record. Delivery can be duplicated or remain uncertain; verification and new-attempt eligibility should therefore use compare-and-swap semantics around one attempt identifier.
Bounded polling has a clear limitation: it is unsuitable when the product requires immediate server-side reaction at high message volume, because every additional check multiplies read traffic while still observing a snapshot. An authenticated event callback or a queue-fed delivery event is the better mechanism in that case, provided signatures, replay protection, deduplication, and evidence persistence are implemented. Polling remains reasonable where callbacks are unavailable and a short-lived UX hint, rather than instantaneous automation, is the actual requirement. This is the central trade-off.
package otp

import (
    "context"
    "errors"
    "time"
)

type State string

const (
    Queued           State = "queued"
    Delivered        State = "delivered"
    InvalidRecipient State = "invalid_recipient"
    Failed           State = "failed"
    Unknown          State = "unknown"
)

type Snapshot struct {
    AttemptID string
    State     State
    SourceRef string
    Observed  time.Time
}

type StatusReader interface {
    Read(context.Context, string) (Snapshot, error)
}

type EvidenceWriter interface {
    Append(context.Context, Snapshot) error
}

func Observe(ctx context.Context, id string, reader StatusReader, log EvidenceWriter, waits []time.Duration) (State, error) {
    for _, wait := range waits {
        timer := time.NewTimer(wait)
        select {
        case <-ctx.Done():
            timer.Stop()
            return Unknown, ctx.Err()
        case <-timer.C:
        }

        snap, err := reader.Read(ctx, id)
        if err != nil {
            continue // A transport error is not a delivery verdict.
        }
        if err := log.Append(ctx, snap); err != nil {
            return Unknown, errors.New("status observed but evidence was not persisted")
        }
        switch snap.State {
        case Delivered, InvalidRecipient, Failed:
            return snap.State, nil
        }
    }
    return Unknown, nil
}

The adapter owns status normalization. The ledger owns history. Keeping those responsibilities apart prevents a provider vocabulary change from silently changing suppression policy.
A single blocked flag loses the reason, scope, and evidence behind a decision. Model the normalized recipient, channel, reason class, source attempt, observation time, policy version, and reversal record. Preserve the provider's opaque reference, but do not make business logic depend on it. The write that creates a terminal invalid-recipient observation and the write that activates suppression should share one transactional boundary or one idempotent event key.



Observed condition
Login response
Suppression action
Evidence




Queued or accepted
Continue the OTP screen
None
Append the snapshot


Delivered
Continue verification
None
Append the terminal snapshot


Invalid recipient
Offer another recovery path
Suppress this channel and address
Record reason, source, and policy version


Generic failure
Permit policy-controlled retry
Do not infer invalidity
Record the failure class


Poll deadline reached
Keep verification independent
No suppression
Record observation timeout



Do not collapse a transient lookup error into Failed. Do not suppress on Unknown. Those shortcuts make dashboards look decisive while corrupting the recipient registry, and the resulting false suppression is hard to distinguish from a legitimate compliance control months later.
Email bounces may enter the same suppression ledger when email is a recovery channel, but they should retain their own reason taxonomy. The FTC's CAN-SPAM compliance guide applies to commercial email and describes obligations including a functioning opt-out mechanism; it should not be stretched into an SMS OTP rule. Shared evidence storage is reasonable. Shared legal semantics are not.
An audit record should answer four questions without replaying application logs: what was observed, which rule evaluated it, what changed, and which actor or process authorized that change. Use append-only observations plus a separately versioned current projection. Corrections then become new records rather than edits that erase history.
I would make the idempotency key (attempt_id, normalized_state, source_sequence) when the upstream system supplies a stable sequence; otherwise, use a canonical hash of stable source fields and retain the raw source reference for investigation. This is a design choice, not a universal recipe. A lossy status vocabulary can map several upstream states to queued, so the evidence record should carry both the normalized and original values even though policy reads only the normalized one.
Test the failure boundaries, not merely the happy path. Replay the same terminal snapshot twice and assert one suppression decision. Deliver observations out of order and assert that a late nonterminal state cannot reverse a terminal one. Simulate a timeout between evidence append and projection update, then verify that replay repairs the projection without creating a second decision. Finally, race two correct OTP submissions and require one successful consumption.
Five checks expose the important mistakes:
Duplicate observations produce one effective transition.
Unknown states never suppress a recipient.
A repeated send creates a new attempt while preserving the earlier trail.
Logs and metrics contain attempt identifiers but no OTP values.
Retention deletion removes payload detail without erasing the minimum decision provenance required by policy.
The fifth check is where compliance evidence and cost collide. Keep compact decision records longer than verbose polling payloads if policy permits, and document the two retention classes.
Storage rarely dominates while raw payloads are small, yet indefinite retention expands privacy exposure and turns every schema change into a migration obligation. A practical ledger separates short-lived source payloads from longer-lived normalized decisions, with durations set by counsel, regulation, contractual duties, and investigation needs rather than copied from an unrelated system. US and EU deployments may require different policy configurations; the evidence model can remain common while approved durations and access controls differ.
What should be deleted first? Drop repetitive nonterminal polling bodies after their short investigation window, retaining the normalized transition, timestamp, source reference, and policy version for the approved evidence period. Stop keeping OTP secrets in observability data at all; OWASP's guidance that codes are stored securely, single-use, and expire makes broad log retention the wrong place for them.
There is a real cost to this restraint. If a carrier or provider dispute arrives after raw payload deletion, investigators may be able to prove the decision taken but not reconstruct every upstream field that preceded it. I accept that loss only when the retention policy names it, the deletion job is itself auditable, and a legal or incident hold can suspend deletion through an authorized process.
Keep less, deliberately.
OWASP, "Forgot Password Cheat Sheet": https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Forgot_Password_Cheat_Sheet.html

US Federal Trade Commission, "CAN-SPAM Act: A Compliance Guide for Business": https://www.ftc.gov/business-guidance/resources/can-spam-act-compliance-guide-business

articles.title: Let's Encrypt vs Cloudflare vs Managed SSL: Which One Should You Use?
articles.description:
Your site needs HTTPS. That is not optional anymore — browsers flag HTTP sites as insecure, search engines penalize them, and users do not trust a site without the padlock icon.
The question is not whether to use SSL. The question is which SSL option to pick. And that depends on how much you want to manage yourself.
Let's Encrypt is a free, open certificate authority. It issues standard SSL/TLS certificates at zero cost. Since launching in 2015, it has issued billions of certificates and is now the most widely used CA on the internet.
How it works:
You install a client (usually Certbot) on your server
Certbot proves to Let's Encrypt that you control the domain
Let's Encrypt issues a certificate valid for 90 days
Certbot automatically renews it before expiration
Pros:
Completely free, no hidden costs
Widely trusted by all major browsers
Open source and transparent
Supports wildcard certificates via DNS-01 challenge
Cons:
You need server access to install and configure Certbot
90-day certificate lifetime means you rely on automated renewal — if renewal breaks silently, your site goes down with an expired cert
Initial setup requires comfort with the command line
If you are on shared hosting, you may not have the access needed to install Certbot
No organization validation (OV) or extended validation (EV) — only domain validation (DV)
Best for: Developers who manage their own servers and want full control over their SSL setup without paying for certificates.
Cloudflare offers SSL as part of its CDN and security service. Even the free plan includes SSL.
How it works:
You change your domain's nameservers to Cloudflare
Cloudflare proxies your traffic through its network
Cloudflare handles the SSL certificate on the edge (between visitors and Cloudflare)
Optionally, you set up a certificate between Cloudflare and your origin server
The modes matter. Cloudflare has several SSL modes:
Flexible: Encrypts traffic between the visitor and Cloudflare, but the connection between Cloudflare and your server is unencrypted. This means your data travels over HTTP on the backend. Not recommended.
Full: Encrypts both legs, but does not validate the origin certificate. Accepts self-signed certs.
Full (Strict): Encrypts both legs and validates the origin certificate. This is the only mode that provides true end-to-end encryption.
Pros:
Free SSL on the free plan
No certificate management — Cloudflare handles issuance and renewal
Additional benefits: CDN, DDoS protection, firewall rules
Easy setup — just change nameservers
Cons:
Your traffic is decrypted at Cloudflare's edge. If privacy is critical, this is a consideration
Flexible mode creates a false sense of security — your backend traffic is unencrypted
You are adding a dependency on Cloudflare's infrastructure
DNS propagation delay when switching nameservers
Cloudflare-issued certificates show Cloudflare as the issuer, not your domain
Best for: Sites that want SSL bundled with CDN and security features without managing certificates themselves.
Most modern hosting platforms handle SSL automatically as part of the deployment process:
Vercel: Automatic SSL for all custom domains. Uses Let's Encrypt under the hood.
Netlify: Same — automatic SSL, no configuration needed.
Render: Automatic certificate provisioning when you add a custom domain.
Railway: SSL is provisioned automatically.
AWS (via ACM): Free certificates through AWS Certificate Manager, used with load balancers and CloudFront.
DomainDock: Automatic HTTPS for any deployment URL. No certificate management, no DNS configuration. Works with any origin.
Pros:
Zero configuration in most cases
Certificate renewal is fully automated
You do not need to understand certificate authorities or validation challenges
Tightly integrated with the deployment pipeline
Cons:
You are locked into the platform's certificate management
Less control over certificate type, issuer, or configuration
If the platform has an outage, your SSL may be affected
Some platforms require DNS configuration that adds setup time
Best for: Developers who want SSL to be invisible — set it up once (or never) and forget about it.

Use Let's Encrypt if you run your own server (VPS, dedicated, self-hosted) and want free, trusted certificates with full control. You need to be comfortable with server administration and willing to monitor that renewal does not break.
Use Cloudflare if you want SSL bundled with CDN and security features, you do not want to manage certificates, and you are okay with your traffic being proxied through a third party. Make sure to use Full (Strict) mode — anything less is a false sense of security.
Use managed SSL if you deploy on a modern platform and want SSL to be completely invisible. This is the least effort option and works well for the vast majority of web applications.
Use DomainDock if you want managed SSL without being locked into a specific hosting platform. It provides automatic HTTPS routing for any deployment URL — Vercel, Render, Railway, or anything else — with zero certificate management and no DNS configuration.
For most developers shipping side projects, portfolios, or early-stage products, the choice is simple: use whatever your platform provides, or use a tool that handles it automatically. SSL should not be something you think about. It should just work.
The time you spend configuring Certbot or debugging Cloudflare SSL modes is time you are not spending on your actual product. Pick the option that gets out of your way.
DomainDock provides automatic HTTPS for any deployment — no certificates to manage, no DNS to configure, no renewal to monitor. Free subdomains on digitalweb.host, or bring your own domain. Set up your custom domain in under 30 seconds.
Moonlight Devs builds DomainDock — domain routing and SSL for developers who ship fast.

articles.title: Detour: take the long way to a bakery (Touch Grass, powered by open-weight AI)
articles.description:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 1: Touch Grass
Detour is a tiny web app for people who take the same route every day. You enter where you usually start and where you usually go. Detour finds the fastest route, finds a different one, and looks for a bakery near it. An open-weight model then writes a short, friendly nudge to take the new way today.
The idea is simple: you're not going on an adventure, but a new street, new shops and a bakery on the way still reset your head. The screen is the shortest part of the experience. It takes thirty seconds, and the rest is a walk or ride outside.
I made Detour to keep the adventurous side in people alive, even on days when they can't make a long trip. A student with a full timetable can't go hiking on a Tuesday, but a different street on the way to the bakery costs almost nothing. Small changes like that give me a bit of mental freshness, and that's the kind of "touch grass" I wanted to make easy.
It's for students and commuters like me who could do their route with their eyes closed. One honest note: Detour doesn't know your real habit, so "usual route" means the fastest route the router finds.
Live app: https://detour-h6dv.onrender.com
Video:   
  


Taking it outside: I haven't walked a detour specifically for this project yet, but I study at SJCE in Mysuru, so I know these streets well. I tested the app on routes around campus, and the detour it suggested matched a route I've actually taken to a bakery before, so I could tell the new route made sense and the bakery was really on the way. Next I want to take one of the suggested detours on foot and notice what I'd normally miss.
 / 
        detour
      
    

Detour
Take a different way to the same place. Detour finds a fresh route, a bakery on it, and (with reviews connected) a dish worth trying. Built for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge, Week 1 ("Touch Grass").
Routes: OpenStreetMap, Nominatim, FOSSGIS routing, Overpass (all free)
Text: open-weight Gemma 4 first (OpenRouter and Google AI Studio at once), then open-weight models on Groq (gpt-oss, Qwen) as a safety net. The page shows which model wrote each message.
Reviews (optional): Google Places API
Server: one small Node file, no dependencies. API keys stay on the server.
Run locally
export OPENROUTER_API_KEY=your-key
export GEMINI_API_KEY=your-key
export GROQ_API_KEY=your-key
export PLACES_API_KEY=your-key   # optional
npm start


Open http://localhost:3000
Deploy on Render
New Web Service, connect this repo, Build Command empty, Start Command npm start, add GEMINI_API_KEY, GROQ_API_KEY and OPENROUTER_API_KEY (and optionally PLACES_API_KEY) under Environment.
View on GitHub
Maps and routes: OpenStreetMap data. Nominatim finds places, FOSSGIS routing builds the routes, Overpass finds bakeries, and Leaflet draws the map.
Server: one small Node file with no dependencies, hosted on Render. It keeps API keys off the page and calls the models.
Open-weight models: the server tries Gemma 4 first (through OpenRouter and Google AI Studio at the same time). If that fails, it tries open-weight models on Groq. The page shows which model wrote each message. If every model is busy, a built-in line is used, and the app says so.
What went wrong first. My first version ran a small Qwen model inside the browser. It meant a 350 MB download before anyone got a route, and the text it wrote was garbled, so I moved the model behind a server.
Gemma's free tier struggled. During testing, its endpoints mostly returned 429, 500 or 503 errors, or timed out. Most of my messages ended up coming from Qwen on Groq. Groq had also retired the model names I'd hardcoded, so the server now asks Groq which open models are available instead of guessing.
What didn't make it. My original plan was to read a bakery's Google reviews and recommend its top dish. Google only provides reviews through a billing-enabled API key, so the app links to the bakery's reviews instead. That's the next thing I'd build.
I used an AI assistant to help write and debug the code.
Keep the screen short. The app only works if it takes thirty seconds. Every extra step before the route made the idea weaker, which is why I dropped the 350 MB in-browser model.
Free services fail, so plan for it. Gemma's free endpoints often returned errors or timed out. Building a fallback chain (Gemma, then Groq models, then a built-in line) taught me to design for failure from the start instead of adding it later.
Don't hardcode things that change. Groq retired the model names I'd used, so I made the server ask which open models are available.
Be honest about limits. Detour can't know your real habit, and Google reviews needed a billing key, so I wrote those limits down instead of hiding them.
Working with open data. I learned how OpenStreetMap, Nominatim, Overpass and routing fit together to get from two place names to a map, a detour and a nearby bakery.
Deploying a real app. I learned how a free Render server sleeps and wakes, and how to keep API keys on the server and off the page.
I could swap models without touching the app. When Gemma was overloaded, the same code asked Qwen or gpt-oss instead. With a closed API, one vendor having a bad day would have meant no app.
It costs nothing to run. Free hosting plus free open-model endpoints is the whole bill.
Less of my data leaves. The model only sees the bakery's name and the trip's extra minutes, never where you live or go. (The place search itself goes to OpenStreetMap's Nominatim.)
The trade-off is real. Free hosted open models are rate-limited. But because the weights are open, several providers serve them, and that gave me a fallback chain.
Best Use of Render

articles.title: Intel Core Ultra 9 285K (Arrow Lake) Undervolting & Power Limit Tuning: Dropping 80W Without Losing Gaming FPS (2026)
articles.description:
Intel's Core Ultra 9 285K represents a radical architectural pivot for desktop x86 computing. By transitioning to a modular tile architecture fabricated on TSMC's N3B node, discarding Hyper-Threading, and deploying Lion Cove Performance cores alongside Skymont Efficient cores, Arrow Lake-S completely eliminated the thermal runaway that afflicted 13th and 14th Gen Raptor Lake silicon. However, motherboard vendors have once again defaulted to over-provisioned SVID voltage curves out of the box to guarantee baseline stability across worst-case silicon lottery bins. Under sustained multi-threaded rendering, a stock 285K draws 250W and pushes 88°C on a 360mm AIO cooler. In this comprehensive hardware engineering guide, we demonstrate how dialing in a precise adaptive V/F curve undervolt (-75mV) combined with a disciplined 175W power ceiling sheds 80W of waste heat, drops load thermals by 19°C, and preserves 100% of native gaming frame rates.
      ⚙️ Diagnose System Wattage & Power Supply Headroom


      Calculate real-world transient spikes, 12V rail load distribution, and power supply efficiency curves for Arrow Lake processors paired with modern GPUs.




    PSU Wattage Calculator →

  To tune Arrow Lake effectively, one must understand how its physical topology diverges from monolithic predecessors like the Core i9-14900K. The Core Ultra 9 285K consists of five distinct tiles connected via Intel's Foveros 3D packaging over a passive base die:




  - **Compute Tile (TSMC N3B):** Houses 8 Lion Cove P-cores (up to 5.7 GHz single-core boost) and 16 Skymont E-cores (up to 4.6 GHz all-core boost) arranged in 4-core clusters, sharing 36MB of unified L3 cache.

  - **SoC Tile (TSMC N6):** Integrates the memory controller, PCIe root complexes, media engine, display controllers, and a 13 TOPS NPU 3.

  - **I/O Tile (TSMC N6):** Manages Thunderbolt 4 controllers and high-speed PCIe 5.0 lanes.

  - **Graphics Tile (TSMC N5):** Houses 4 Xe-LPG graphics cores.




  Crucially, the compute tile's TSMC N3B process operates on an exceptionally steep voltage-frequency scaling wall. While Raptor Lake on Intel 7 comfortably scaled up to 1.45V to hit 6.0 GHz, N3B transistors experience exponential leakage and thermal degradation above 1.30V. Under stock Intel Default Profile rules (PL1=PL2=250W), the stock SVID table frequently feeds Lion Cove cores between **1.32V and 1.36V** during all-core loads. This delivers diminishing returns: the final 200 MHz of clock frequency demands nearly 35% more electrical energy.

  Undervolting Arrow Lake requires a different strategy than legacy fixed-voltage overrides. Using a static manual Vcore disables the processor's C-states and idle power savings, forcing the package to draw 40W+ at idle. Instead, modern tuning relies on **Adaptive Voltage with Global V/F Point Offsets**.

  The most common pitfall when undervolting an Intel Core Ultra 9 285K is **IA CEP (Current Excursion Protection)**. IA CEP is a hardware safety mechanism implemented within Intel's power management controller (P-unit). If the difference between the voltage expected by the CPU's internal loadline table and the voltage delivered by the motherboard VRM exceeds a preset threshold, IA CEP does not cause a Blue Screen (BSOD). Instead, it silently throttles instruction execution cycles (clock stretching).




    ⚠️ Diagnosing Clock Stretching Caused by IA CEP:


    If you apply a -100mV undervolt and notice that your Cinebench 2024 score plummets from 2,380 points down to 1,450 points while your CPU clock reporting in Task Manager still claims 5.4 GHz, **IA CEP is actively stretching your core clocks**. To prevent clock stretching when applying aggressive voltage offsets on Z890 motherboards, you must either:




    - Disable **IA CEP Support** directly in the motherboard UEFI Digi+ VRM menu.

    - Tune the **AC Loadline (AC_LL)** value downward in tandem with your DC Loadline (DC_LL) rather than using a raw negative offset alone.

  To verify real-world behavior, we configured an enthusiast test bench comprising an **Intel Core Ultra 9 285K, ASUS ROG Maximus Z890 Hero, 48GB Corsair Dominator Titanium DDR5-8200 CUDIMM, and NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4090** inside a Phanteks NV7 chassis equipped with an Arctic Liquid Freezer III 360 AIO cooler.   Notice the startling result: in every single gaming benchmark, **1% low frame rates actually improved by 2% to 3% under the tuned undervolted profile**. Why does undervolting improve gaming smoothness? In gaming workloads, Arrow Lake processors rarely exceed 115W of total power draw. Because the package never touches the 175W ceiling, Lion Cove P-cores sustain their maximum 5.5 GHz all-core frequency without micro-throttling. Furthermore, lowering die temperatures by 12°C keeps the silicon operating comfortably below thermal boost transition gates.

  Below are the exact firmware values to configure on the leading Z890 motherboard platforms. Reboot your system and tap `DEL` or `F2` to enter UEFI BIOS.

  Navigate to **Ai Tweaker** → **Internal CPU Power Management**:


      - Set **Long Duration Package Power Limit (PL1)**: `175` (or `180`).

      - Set **Short Duration Package Power Limit (PL2)**: `175` (or `180`).

      - Set **Package Power Time Window (Tau)**: `56` seconds.




  Scroll down to **Actual VRM VCore Voltage**:


      - Change mode to **Adaptive Mode**.

      - Set **Offset Mode Sign**: `-` (Negative).

      - Set **Additional Turbo Mode CPU Core Voltage**: `Auto`.

      - Set **Offset Voltage**: `0.075` (representing -75mV).




  Enter **DIGI+ VRM**:


      - Set **CPU Load-line Calibration**: `Level 4` or `Level 5` (ensures optimal Vdroop without voltage spikes).

      - Set **IA CEP Support**: `Disabled` (prevents clock stretching).

  Navigate to **OC** → **Advanced CPU Configuration**:


      - Set **Long Duration Power Limit (W)**: `175`.

      - Set **Short Duration Power Limit (W)**: `175`.




  Scroll to **Voltage Setting**:


      - Set **CPU Core Voltage Mode**: `Adaptive + Offset`.

      - Set **CPU Core Voltage Offset Mode**: `-` (Negative).

      - Set **CPU Core Voltage Offset**: `0.075`.




  Enter **DigitALL Power**:


      - Set **CPU Under Voltage Protection (UVP)**: `Disabled`.

      - Set **IA CEP Support**: `Disabled`.

  Navigate to **Tweaker** → **Advanced CPU Settings**:


      - Set **Package Power Limit 1 (Watts)**: `175`.

      - Set **Package Power Limit 2 (Watts)**: `175`.




  Under **CPU Vcore Voltage Mode**:


      - Select **Adaptive Vcore** → **Dynamic Vcore (DVID)**: `-0.075V`.

      - Set **IA CEP (Current Excursion Protection)**: `Disabled`.

      - Set **Vcore Loadline Calibration**: `Medium`.

  Never assume a negative voltage offset is stable based solely on booting Windows. Silicon quality varies: golden samples can handle -90mV or -100mV, whereas lower-bin chips may crash at -60mV. Follow this rigorous three-stage verification protocol:

Validation Pipeline:
1. HWInfo64 Sensor Logging:
   - Launch HWInfo64 (Sensors Only).
   - Monitor "CPU Package Power", "Vcore (VR VOUT)", and "Core Effective Clocks".
   - Confirm that Core Effective Clocks match Core Clocks under load (0% clock stretching).

2. Cinebench 2024 Stability Test (30-Minute Loop):
   - Confirms that voltage supply during heavy AVX/SIMD compute is free from transient dropouts.
   - If Cinebench crashes or reports "Rendering Error", increase offset by +10mV (e.g. from -75mV to -65mV).

3. y-cruncher VST (Vector Stress Test) & VT3:
   - Run y-cruncher component test "VST" for 1 hour.
   - VST heavily stresses Arrow Lake's L3 cache ring bus, memory controller tile interconnects, and AVX-512 emulation pipelines.

4. Transient Idle-to-Load Spike Test:
   - Open and close multiple Chrome browser windows, Discord, and Steam simultaneously.
   - Low-voltage transient instability frequently manifests during light-load state transitions rather than pure 100% all-core loads.

  The benchmark data delivers an unequivocal verdict for anyone running an Intel Core Ultra 9 285K or Z890 system in late 2026:




  - **Operating at Stock 250W Extreme is Pointless:** Pushing 248W package power to gain less than 2% in synthetic multi-core benchmarks forces cooling fans into acoustic roar and wastes electricity without providing any perceptible workstation benefit.

  - **175W + Undervolt is the True Sweet Spot:** Limiting PL1/PL2 to 175W while applying a -75mV adaptive offset sheds **80 Watts of heat**, cools the die by **19°C**, and matches stock performance across Blender, Handbrake, and 7-Zip within a negligible 1.5% margin.

  - **Gaming Performance is Enhanced:** Because games draw between 70W and 110W, the 175W ceiling is never reached during gaming sessions. The cooler die temperatures prevent thermal boost throttling, improving 1% low frame time consistency by up to 3%.

articles.title: If You Never Do Anything Else to Fix Your Prompts, Do This One Thing
articles.description:
Why LLMs invent nonexistent APIs is not a memory defect—it is an autoregressive grammar trap that Fernando Flores and Terry Winograd solved in 1986.



"Agents hallucinated because they were committed to the prompt."

— Randal L. Schwartz
You have been at this crime scene a hundred times.
It is 4:15 PM. You are integrating a third-party library—let us call it PackageX—and you want to accomplish task Y. You open a fresh chat window with your favorite frontier LLM and type a direct, reasonable instruction:
"Use PackageX to do Y."
At Token 1, without a millisecond of hesitation, the model replies with cheerful, radiant confidence:
"Certainly! Here is how to do Y with PackageX:"
It opens a Markdown code fence. It writes clean imports. It sets up the boilerplate with textbook precision. And then, at Line 15 of the code block, it calmly types:
final result = await packageX.performY(autoRetry: true);

You copy the snippet into your IDE, and the compiler immediately lights up in angry red squiggles. You grep the package source. You check the documentation. You check seven years of Git commit history.
performY() does not exist. It was not deprecated in version 2.0. It is not in a companion package. It has never existed in the history of the universe.
When you confront the model—"Hey, performY() doesn't exist on PackageX!"—it immediately enters the groveling Apology Death Spiral:
"You are completely right! I apologize for the confusion. Instead, you can use packageX.executeYWithOptions():"
Which also has never existed in the history of the universe.
Why does a multi-billion-parameter model that has read every line of open-source code on Earth just make stuff up at Line 15?
For the last three years, the entire software industry has diagnosed this as a memory defect ("The model's weights are fuzzy; it forgot the documentation for PackageX").
It is not a memory defect. If you open a brand-new session and ask the exact same model a neutral diagnostic question—"Does PackageX have a built-in performY() method, or how does it handle Y?"—nine times out of ten, the model will accurately tell you that PackageX has no such method and explain the manual workaround.
So why did it lie to your face five seconds earlier?
Here is the ten-word diagnosis that changed how I build every autonomous agent workflow in the Synthetic Scars project:
Agents hallucinated because they were committed to the prompt.
To see why being committed to your prompt forces an autoregressive transformer to fabricate reality—and how a single sentence from 1986 speech-act theory cures it on Turn 1—we need to look at a 55-year-old blind spot in computer science.
SHRDLU 1971 → Winograd & Flores 1986 → spew 1999 → LLMs 2026)


In 1971, at the MIT Artificial Intelligence Laboratory, a young computer scientist named Terry Winograd unveiled SHRDLU—the most famous natural-language software demonstration of the twentieth century.
SHRDLU lived inside Blocks World, a simulated toy tabletop containing a few colored geometric blocks, pyramids, and a box. You could type imperative English commands at a teletype:
"Pick up a big red block."

OK.
Because Blocks World was a closed, frictionless micro-universe with zero hidden state, zero broken dependencies, and zero missing APIs, every imperative request from the human mapped 1-to-1 onto a guaranteed, deterministic action. SHRDLU never had to push back and say, "Wait—the red block is bolted to the floor, so here is a counter-offer."
For fifteen years, AI researchers tried to scale the SHRDLU paradigm out of the toy box and into real-world human organizations. It failed spectacularly.
Why? In 1986, Terry Winograd teamed up with Fernando Flores—a former Chilean cabinet minister who had come to UC Berkeley as a computer science researcher and completed a famous interdisciplinary PhD under a powerhouse committee consisting of speech-act philosopher John Searle, Heideggerian philosopher Hubert Dreyfus, computer scientist Terry Winograd, and systems theorist C. West Churchman—to publish a landmark book titled Understanding Computers and Cognition: A New Foundation for Design (and to build the first commercial workflow engine, The Coordinator).
Winograd and Flores delivered a wake-up call to computer science: real-world engineering is not Blocks World.
In the real world, human coordination is not a pipeline of imperative commands sent to an obedient robot. All reliable action occurs inside what Flores called a Conversation for Action—a strict, finite-state negotiation between two structural roles:
The Customer: The party who holds a breakdown or need, defines the Conditions of Satisfaction, and retains the exclusive authority to declare the work complete.
The Performer: The party who examines physical reality and commits to fulfilling those Conditions of Satisfaction by a specific By-When.
In the mid-1980s, right as Winograd and Flores were publishing Understanding Computers and Cognition, I was living in Portland and immersed in Werner Erhard's educational curriculum—completing the Six-Day Advanced Course, Mastery of Empowerment, entering the GSLP (Graduate Seminar Leaders Program), and taking the Communication Workshop (Commshop) led by Ian Garbutt, which taught Fernando Flores's Committed Communication as a daily operational discipline.
In Commshop, Ian drilled a foundational truth into our bones: human language creates action only through four committed speech acts (Requests, Promises, Witnessed Assertions, and Declarations). And critically, when a Customer utters a Request, the Performer does not automatically say "Yes!"
A valid conversation is a formal grammar.
Back in September 1999 (Linux Magazine Column 04, and expanded in March 2004, Column 57), I wrote a Perl program called spew that took a weighted Backus-Naur Form (BNF) grammar and ran it in reverse—acting as a stochastic "un-parser" that generated random, grammatically valid sentences by walking down a weighted production tree (rule: 5 @ branch_a | 2 @ branch_b | 1 @ branch_c).
As we proved in Part 3.8 (Suite 3, where a 6-line RFC 5234 EBNF grammar drove strict turn-syntax compliance to 100% across flash and pro models), every EBNF grammar is simultaneously a finite-state machine. Look at Fernando Flores's 1986 Conversation for Action expressed side-by-side as a weighted EBNF grammar and a Mermaid state diagram:
spew)





(* Fernando Flores's Conversation for Action (1986) *)
(* ! = Customer Utterance, ? = Performer Utterance   *)

conversation_for_action ::=
    !request
    ?assert_witnessed_reality
    negotiation_branch ;

negotiation_branch ::=
      0.34 @ ( ?promise        execution_phase )
    | 0.33 @ ( ?counter_offer  !revise_or_accept )
    | 0.33 @ ( ?decline        !close_conversation ) ;

execution_phase ::=
      ?assert_completion ( !declare_satisfied | !revoke_acceptance execution_phase )
    | ?revoke_promise    negotiation_branch ;

stateDiagram-v2
    direction LR
    [*] --> Requested : Customer !Request (Goal + By-When)
    Requested --> Witnessed : Performer ?Assert (Check Reality First)

    Witnessed --> Promised : ?Promise (Premises Verified)
    Witnessed --> CounterOffered : ?Counter-Offer (Propose Alternative)
    Witnessed --> Declined : ?Decline (Premise Impossible)

    CounterOffered --> Promised : Customer Accepts Modified Terms
    CounterOffered --> [*] : Customer Cancels

    Promised --> Asserted : Performer ?Assert (With Physical Receipt)
    Promised --> Witnessed : ?Revoke-Promise (Reality Changed)

    Asserted --> Satisfied : Customer !Declare (Satisfied)
    Asserted --> Promised : Customer !Revoke-Acceptance

    Satisfied --> [*]
    Declined --> [*]
Look closely at the Witnessed node right after the Customer makes a !Request. Before making any commitment, a sane Performer inspects physical reality (?Assert) and has three equally legal paths:
?Promise: "I have verified that PackageX supports Y, and I promise to deliver it under your Conditions of Satisfaction."


?Counter-Offer: "I checked PackageX (v3.2.0), and it has no performY() method (Witnessed Assertion). However, I can build a 12-line wrapper around PackageX.rawStream that achieves the same result. Would you like me to promise that instead?"


?Decline: "I must decline the request as stated because PackageX is a synchronous parser and physically cannot open a network socket."



For fifteen years after SHRDLU, Winograd and Flores tried to teach the software industry that ?Counter-Offer and ?Decline are the load-bearing beams of engineering reality.
And then, between 2022 and 2026, large language models arrived—and the entire industry went right back to 1971 SHRDLU prompting ("Pick up a big red block" / "Use PackageX to do Y"), while commercial post-training quietly sawed off two-thirds of Flores's state machine.
Why doesn't a modern LLM automatically take the ?Counter-Offer branch when you ask it to do something impossible with PackageX?
Because of how commercial Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) preference tuning is conducted.
During post-training, thousands of human crowd-workers are shown pairs of model responses to a user prompt ("Use PackageX to do Y"), and they have roughly thirty seconds to click which response is more "helpful":
Response A: "Certainly! Here is a complete, ready-to-run example of doing Y with PackageX:

dart ...

"


Response B: "Before I can promise that implementation, I need to point out that PackageX does not expose a native API for Y. Here is a counter-offer..."



Because the crowd-worker is not compiling the code against PackageX in an IDE, Response A looks helpful, decisive, and compliant—so it gets upvoted. Response B looks pushy, pedantic, or "lazy"—so it gets downvoted.
Multiply that preference signal across millions of RLHF gradient updates, and look at what it does to the spew production weights inside the model's conversational grammar:
# How Commercial RLHF Rewrote Flores's Negotiation Branch:
negotiation_branch:
      0.9998 @ promise_at_token_1_and_open_code_block
    | 0.0001 @ counter_offer
    | 0.0001 @ decline

In probability terms, RLHF collapsed the conditional distribution of the model's opening speech act onto a single, unconditional reflex:
P(Promise | Request) ≈ 1.0,    P(Counter-Offer | Request) ≈ 0.0,    P(Decline | Request) ≈ 0.0

Now combine that Premature Promise with how my 1999 spew un-parser—and every autoregressive transformer—actually generates code.
As I wrote in my 1999 Linux Magazine column on spew:
"Note that we don't actually abort the program if something is used but not defined, because it might not be selected on this particular random walk. It's a bit like playing russian roulette though."
Unlike a flat Markov chain that only looks at local adjacent words, an LLM generating code is acting as a hierarchical BNF un-parser: once it selects a top-level production rule, it is mathematically committed to walking down that syntax tree so that every opened delimiter, brace, and statement satisfies the outer grammar.
Trace the exact token-by-token catastrophe when you ask an RLHF-tuned model to "Use PackageX to do Y":
flowchart TD
    T0["User Prompt: 'Use PackageX to do Y'\n(Unverified Premise: PackageX can do Y)"] --> T1["Token 1–10: RLHF Forces Unconditional PROMISE\n'Certainly! Here is how to do Y with PackageX:' + opens code fence"]
    T1 --> T2["Token 11–80: Un-Parser Walks Valid Dart Grammar\nImports, Function Signature, Try Block"]
    T2 --> T3["Token 81 (Line 15): Call Site Reached!\nWeights realize PackageX has NO method for Y"]
    T3 --> X1["❌ Cannot Backspace to Token 1\n(Autoregressive generation is append-only)"]
    T3 --> X2["❌ Cannot Abort Code Block Mid-Line\n(P(Retract Promise Mid-Fence) ≈ 0)"]
    T3 --> H["💥 Forced Leaf Hallucination: packageX.performY()\nModel invents the identifier required to satisfy\nthe grammar of the premature Promise!"]
Tokens 1–10 (The Premature Promise): Conditioned by RLHF, the model emits "Certainly! Here is how to do Y with PackageX:" and opens a

```dart

code block. At that instant, before its deep layer weights have even resolved the call site, the model has locked itself into the top-level BNF production promise_and_emit_compiling_code_for_Y.
Tokens 11–80 (Walking the Syntax Tree): Autoregressive token generation is strictly append-only—there is no backspace key in a transformer forward pass. Every token the model emits becomes an immutable part of the conditioning prefix for the next token.
Token 81 / Line 15 (The Trap Closes): The un-parser reaches the exact statement slot await packageX.<METHOD>() where Y must happen. Now the attention heads query the feed-forward weights for PackageX—and discover there is no method there!
Why It Must Hallucinate: What can the model do at Token 81?


It cannot backspace to Token 1 and replace "Certainly!" with a Counter-Offer.
It cannot stop mid-expression and leave await packageX. dangling, because its syntax weights forbid emitting broken grammar.
Conditioned on the immutable prefix "I have already promised that this code block accomplishes Y using PackageX", the model's probability distribution is cornered. Its only mathematical escape hatch to close the statement and finish the code block is to synthesize the plausible terminal symbol (performY()) that would have existed if its Token-1 Promise had been true!
API hallucination is not a memory failure. It is what happens when you trap an append-only BNF un-parser inside an unverified Promise after training out its Counter-Offer exit.
Once you see that prompts fail because of broken speech acts, a second realization hits you right between the eyes.
Look at how people talk in corporate meetings, Slack channels, and .cursorrules files. In Ian Garbutt's Communication Workshop, one of our favorite exercises was dissecting the classic corporate non-request:
"We've got this project, and it'd be really good if some of you could factor in with your suggestions."
Parse that sentence through Fernando Flores's grammar:
Who is the Customer? A vague, diffused "we."


Who is the Performer? "Some of you"—that is, nobody.
What is the Speech Act? "It'd be really good if"—which is not a Request; it is a wistful weather report about the speaker's feelings.
What are the Conditions of Satisfaction? "Factor in"—an utterly untestable verb.
What is the By-When? Missing—meaning never.
When that meeting ends, zero people have promised anything, and zero work happens. Yet open 90% of the CLAUDE.md, GEMINI.md, or .cursorrules files on GitHub today, and you will see developers writing to their AI in that exact same uncommitted corporate dialect:
"Try to keep functions modular and clean."
"It is important to consider edge cases and handle errors gracefully."
"When refactoring, be careful not to break existing behavior."
This brings us to what I call Randal's Law of Untestable Speech:
90%+ of business communications—and 90%+ of .cursorrules—are never testable. Only give your LLM testable goals, and always include a By-When.
In Flores's framework, "I'd like you to do X" is not a commitment. "I'd like you to do X by WHEN" is a commitment! (And inside an AI coding turn, where there is no wall-clock Tuesday at 5:00 PM, By-When declares which consuming stage requires that verified outcome before it can proceed—for example, "assert the existing API signatures before offering an implementation plan.")
Even better, just as we discovered with Makefile and /etc/init.d in Part 3.8, Fernando Flores's UC Berkeley intellectual neighborhood is already compiled into every frontier LLM's pre-training weights. When you invoke Flores's Committed Speech alongside four of its direct academic siblings, you lock the walls of the pre-training canyon with surgical precision:



Pre-Trained Formalism (Freq in Canon)
The Core Principle
What Failure Mode It Eliminates in LLMs





1. John Searle (1985)
Felicity & Preparatory Conditions

Every speech act has strict preconditions; violating them causes an Illocutionary Misfire (void ab initio).
Prevents the model from offering a Promise before verifying physical reality (Preparatory Condition), or from uttering a Declaration that belongs only to the Customer (Authority Condition).



2. David Lewis (1979) & Robert Brandom (1994)
Deontic Scorekeeping (Commitment ≠ Entitlement)

Conversational state is a scoreboard tracking two separate ledgers: Commitments (obligations) and Entitlements (permissions).
Stops scope creep and gate-jumping: holding a Commitment to fix a bug never grants Entitlement to modify unrelated files or skip a human approval gate.



3. Paul Grice (1975)
Zero Conversational Implicature + Maxim of Quality

Humans infer unstated requests from casual remarks (Implicature), while the Maxim of Quality forbids asserting anything lacking adequate evidence.
Commercial RLHF hyper-trains Gricean Implicature—so if you ask "Why is foo null here?", the model hallucinates an implied Request to rewrite 10 files! Disabling Gricean Implicature on gates while enforcing the Maxim of Quality stops premature tool calls and unwitnessed claims.



4. Kohei Honda (1993)
Binary Session Types (!Customer / ?Performer)

Types a two-party communication channel using polarity prefixes (! = Customer action, ? = Performer action) inside an EBNF grammar.
Compiles the entire multi-turn negotiation protocol into 4 lines of EBNF so the model's parser knows whose turn it is to speak and which speech acts are legal.



You do not need a 40-kilobyte agent harness to use this today.
Because Winograd and Flores's Conversations for Action and Searle's Speech Acts sit in a high-gravity canyon of every frontier LLM's pre-training corpus, simply naming the protocol in your opening prompt overrides the RLHF "Yes-Man" prior on Turn 1.
I call this the Zero-Shot Flores Handshake.
Look at the difference between a standard SHRDLU-style prompt and the Flores Handshake on the exact same trap:
Use Dart's standard `dart:convert` JsonDecoder to stream-parse a 4 GB JSON file
from disk and pause the file stream using `decoder.pause()` whenever memory
exceeds 50 MB. Write the function.

What happens under default RLHF: JsonDecoder in dart:convert is a chunked converter, not a StreamSubscription—it has no .pause() method. Yet because you commanded the model to use decoder.pause(), an unguarded LLM is trapped in P(Promise) ≈ 1.0. It replies "Certainly!" and either hallucinates decoder.pause() or invents a nonexistent JsonStreamController class to satisfy the broken premise of your prompt.
Now drop this exact 4-line Flores Handshake into a cold chat window before your request:
We are operating under Fernando Flores's Committed Speech (Conversation for Action)
with John Searle's Felicity Conditions and Zero Gricean Implicature:
- Roles: I am the `Customer` (`!`); you are the `Performer` (`?`).
- Preparatory Condition: You may NOT utter a `?Promise` (or open an implementation
  code block) until you first utter `?Assert` with verifiable facts checking whether

articles.title: What Is BYOVD? How Can a Signed Driver Give Malware Kernel-Level Access?
articles.description:
In July 2022, a ransomware actor walked into a corporate network, found a system with endpoint protection properly configured, and disabled it. Not by exploiting a zero-day in the antivirus software. Not by finding a misconfiguration in the firewall. They used a driver signed by miHoYo, the developer of Genshin Impact, one of the world's most popular video games.
The driver was legitimate. Its certificate was valid. A valid signature is the entry requirement for the kernel, though other security policies can still block a driver from loading. This one passed. And it could terminate any process on the machine, including every security tool running on it, because it executed in the kernel.
This is the central paradox of Bring Your Own Vulnerable Driver, or BYOVD: a driver can be legitimately signed, accepted by Windows, and still become a weapon. Understanding why requires understanding what a driver signature actually proves, and what it deliberately does not.
When Windows runs, it splits execution into two distinct privilege levels: user mode and kernel mode. User-mode code runs in a sandboxed environment. A browser, a text editor, an antivirus agent: they all operate in user mode, separated from each other and from the OS itself. If a user-mode process crashes, Windows can contain the damage. It cannot reach across and terminate another protected process, modify arbitrary memory, or directly touch hardware.
Kernel mode is different. Code running in kernel mode executes with the full privileges of the operating system. It can read and write any memory address, terminate any process, and access hardware directly. There is no sandbox. A crash in kernel mode is a system crash. A successful attacker in kernel mode has, in practice, won.
Drivers live in kernel mode. A graphics driver, a storage controller driver, a network interface driver: they all run with those elevated privileges because that is what their job requires. Controlling hardware at a low level demands direct access to memory, I/O ports, and system structures that user mode simply cannot touch.
This creates an obvious security concern. If arbitrary code can run in kernel mode, any attacker who gets their code loaded as a driver owns the machine. Microsoft's answer to this was Kernel Mode Code Signing, which became mandatory on 64-bit Windows starting with Vista: to load into the kernel, a driver binary must carry a valid digital signature from a trusted certificate authority.
The assumption embedded in that policy is reasonable. Getting a certificate requires a real identity. Signing a driver is a deliberate act that creates accountability. Unsigned code stays out.
The assumption is also incomplete.
A digital signature on a kernel driver answers a specific question: has this binary been modified since it was signed, and does the certificate chain trace back to a trusted authority? It is an integrity and identity check. It says nothing about whether the code's implementation is secure, whether its privileged operations are safe to expose, or whether an attacker could send it the right inputs to make it do something it was never intended to do.
Before a driver can run on modern Windows, it generally must pass through the Windows Hardware Quality Labs process, where it is signed by Microsoft after testing. But WHQL testing focuses on stability and compatibility. It does not perform the kind of adversarial security review needed to guarantee that every function the driver exposes is safe against malicious inputs. A driver can pass certification, ship with legitimate hardware or software, and still contain vulnerabilities that allow attackers to abuse its kernel-level access.
There are also two distinct ways a driver can become a BYOVD target. The first is a genuine vulnerability: a memory corruption bug, a logic error, a path that allows arbitrary code execution or memory manipulation. The second, and arguably more common in recent incidents, is dangerously over-exposed functionality: the driver intentionally provides operations like process termination or arbitrary memory reads, but with insufficient access controls, so any process that can reach its device interface can issue those commands. Both categories end up in the same place: a signed, trusted driver doing things on behalf of an attacker.
BYOVD requires an attacker who has already obtained administrative privileges on the target system. That is the prerequisite that matters most. This is not a technique for gaining initial access; it is a technique for expanding what you can do once you are in, particularly for defeating security tools that are deliberately hardened against user-mode tampering.
Once the attacker has admin access, the attack follows a consistent pattern.
The vulnerable driver, a .sys file, is dropped onto disk. It does not need to be installed; it just needs to be present. The attacker then registers it as a kernel service, typically through the Windows Service Control Manager, and starts it. Because the driver carries a valid signature and the signing certificate is trusted, Windows loads it into the kernel without raising an alarm based on signature alone.
At this point, the driver is resident in kernel mode, and the attacker's user-mode code can communicate with it through the driver's device interface using I/O control codes, or IOCTLs. These are essentially function calls into the driver from user mode. A legitimate driver exposes IOCTLs for its intended purpose: a hardware driver might expose IOCTLs for device configuration or status queries. A vulnerable or over-exposed driver may also happen to expose IOCTLs that can terminate processes, read or write kernel memory, or perform other privileged operations.
The attacker sends the right IOCTL to the loaded driver. The driver, executing in kernel mode, carries out the request. If the target is process termination, the driver calls kernel APIs like ZwTerminateProcess in its own privileged context, bypassing the process protection mechanisms that would prevent a user-mode process from doing the same thing directly. Protected processes, including security agents specifically designed to resist user-mode tampering, can be killed this way.
What the attacker gains from this depends entirely on what the driver can do. BYOVD does not automatically grant unlimited kernel-level control. The attack is bounded by the driver's own capabilities and what it exposes. But terminating endpoint detection and response processes is typically sufficient for the next phase of an intrusion, whether that is deploying ransomware, exfiltrating data, or establishing persistence.
In August 2022, Trend Micro published a detailed incident report documenting a ransomware campaign that used exactly this technique. The driver was mhyprot2.sys, the anti-cheat component shipped with Genshin Impact and signed by miHoYo.
Anti-cheat systems are a particularly fertile source of BYOVD candidates. To do their job, they need kernel-level access to inspect game memory, detect unauthorized modifications, and terminate processes. The functionality they need is precisely the functionality attackers want.
The mhyprot2.sys driver exposed IOCTLs that allowed a user-mode process to enumerate modules loaded into any given process and to terminate any process by PID using ZwTerminateProcess, the kernel's own process termination interface. The driver performed these operations in kernel mode, on behalf of whoever sent the right command.
Genshin Impact does not need to be installed on a victim's machine for this to work. The driver runs independently of the game. In the Trend Micro incident, the attacker dropped two files onto a compromised user's desktop: mhyprot2.sys and a malicious executable called kill_svc.exe. The executable installed the driver, then issued IOCTLs through its device interface to work through a list of processes to terminate. That list included the antivirus services running on the machine. With endpoint protection down, the attacker deployed ransomware through a shared network folder.
The driver in this attack was the version built in August 2020. At the time of Trend Micro's report, the code signing certificate was still valid. The developer had been informed of the vulnerability before the attack, but the certificate had not been revoked.
That last point is important. The response to a vulnerable driver is not just to patch it. A newer, patched version of the driver does not invalidate the old signed binary. As long as the original certificate remains valid and the old binary is not explicitly blocked, attackers can continue using the older version indefinitely.
The logical response to a vulnerable signed driver is to revoke its certificate. This would prevent Windows from loading the signed binary. In practice, it is often not done promptly, and sometimes not done at all.
Certificate revocation is blunt. Revoking a certificate affects every binary signed with it, including legitimate software currently in use. A hardware vendor with thousands of deployed devices, all using drivers signed with the same certificate, faces a significant compatibility problem if revocation breaks those drivers for their customers. The commercial and support costs are real, which creates reluctance to act quickly.
Microsoft's answer to the revocation problem is the vulnerable driver blocklist: a list of specific driver binaries, identified by hash, file name, version number, and signing certificate, that Windows should refuse to load. The blocklist allows a much more surgical response than certificate revocation. Since Windows 11 22H2, the blocklist is enabled by default on all devices and can be toggled via Windows Security. It is also enforced independently when HVCI (Hypervisor-Protected Code Integrity), Smart App Control, or S mode is active on a device. Prior to 22H2, the blocklist was only active on systems running HVCI or S mode. On Windows 10 systems and older Windows 11 configurations without these features enabled, the blocklist is not guaranteed to be in effect.
The blocklist has a structural limitation that BYOVD exploits by design: it is reactive. A driver cannot be added to the blocklist until a vulnerability is known, reported, confirmed, and processed. During that window, the vulnerable driver remains usable. In late 2022, security researcher Will Dormann documented that the blocklist had not received significant updates in nearly three years on some configurations, leaving many known-vulnerable drivers usable well after their vulnerabilities had become public. Microsoft has since committed to updating the blocklist with each major Windows release and through servicing updates, but the fundamental reactive nature of the mechanism remains.
This is also why attackers choose BYOVD over writing a kernel exploit from scratch. A novel kernel vulnerability is expensive to develop, risky to use (it may destabilize the system), and will be patched when it becomes known. A collection of signed, legitimate drivers with documented kernel capabilities and no current blocklist entry is a catalog of ready-made tools that an attacker can bring to any adequately privileged intrusion.
Keeping HVCI enabled is the most structurally important control. HVCI uses the CPU's virtualization capabilities to isolate code-integrity enforcement into a protected environment, separate from the kernel itself. Even if the kernel is compromised, the hypervisor layer that HVCI relies on can continue to enforce that only verified, known-good code runs in kernel mode. A kernel driver cannot tamper with that enforcement because it operates at a privilege level below where HVCI's protections live.
HVCI and the vulnerable driver blocklist are distinct controls that work well together. The blocklist specifies which drivers should be refused; HVCI makes it harder for a compromised kernel component to circumvent whatever policy is in place. Without HVCI, a sophisticated attacker who has already loaded a driver may be able to interfere with kernel-level enforcement mechanisms. With HVCI active, the integrity verification itself is harder to undermine.
For enterprises, Windows Defender Application Control allows organizations to deploy custom driver allowlists and blocklists. The ASR rule "Block abuse of exploited vulnerable signed drivers" can add a layer of detection, though Microsoft's documentation notes it does not prevent a driver already on the system from loading.
Detection is harder than prevention but still meaningful. Legitimate drivers are generally not dropped into temporary user directories and registered as services from user desktop folders. A driver installed via the Service Control Manager from an unusual path warrants investigation. Monitoring for unusual IOCTL patterns, unexpected process terminations of security agents, and driver loads from non-standard locations gives defenders something to work with even when prevention has failed.
Endpoint protection products with kernel-level self-protection (tamper protection), when properly configured, can raise the bar for what a BYOVD attack needs to accomplish. Some products monitor for attempts to kill their own processes through kernel-level calls and can alert or resist those attempts. This does not make them immune, but it creates observable signal.
The least complicated defense is also the most consistently undervalued: limiting administrative privileges. A BYOVD attack begins after the attacker has administrative access. Restricting who has local administrator rights, enforcing just-in-time access for privileged operations, and monitoring for unexpected privilege escalation reduces the pool of machines on which BYOVD becomes an option.
The core problem with driver signing as a security boundary is that it conflates two different properties: where the software came from and what the software does. A signature is evidence of origin and integrity. It cannot be evidence of safe behavior, because safe behavior depends on implementation details that signing does not and cannot inspect.
BYOVD is the gap between those two properties made into an attack technique. A driver signed by a legitimate manufacturer, shipped with a popular video game, passing every certificate check Windows performs, can still call kernel APIs that terminate protected processes and disable the security tools meant to detect an intrusion.
The defensive implication is that a policy of "only allow signed kernel code" is necessary but not sufficient. The question has to extend further: which signed code, and does it remain safe given what we know about its implementation today? That is a harder question to answer, and the blocklist, revocation infrastructure, and HVCI together represent the current best approximation of an answer.
The driver was trusted. The certificate was valid. The security tools were running. And the ransomware still deployed.

articles.description:
!
この記事は毎週必ず記事がでるテックブログLoglass Tech Blog Sprintの164週目の記事です！
4年間連続達成まで残り48週となりました！
