Securing the Software Supply Chain: Generating SBOMs & SLSA Provenance in GitLab CI/CD


From the SolarWinds breach to the recent XZ Utils backdoor, software supply chain attacks have moved from theoretical risks to frontline security crises.
It is no longer enough to verify that your own proprietary code is clean. Regulators, enterprise buyers, and security frameworks (like NIST SP 800-218, Executive Order 14028, and FedRAMP) now mandate:
Software Bill of Materials (SBOM): An exact, machine-readable inventory of every third-party package and transitive dependency shipped inside your binaries and containers.
SLSA Build Provenance (Supply-chain Levels for Software Artifacts): Cryptographic proof of where, when, and by what git commit a binary artifact was compiled.
Fortunately, GitLab provides built-in, native support for both CycloneDX SBOM generation and automated SLSA provenance attestations.
In this guide, I will show you how to configure a production-grade software supply chain security pipeline in GitLab CI/CD.
+-------------------------------------------------------------+
|                      git push (Signed Commit)               |
+-------------------------------------------------------------+
                              |
                              v
+-------------------------------------------------------------+
|                     GitLab CI/CD Runner                     |
+-------------------------------------------------------------+
         |                                             |
         v                                             v
+------------------------------+     +-------------------------------+
|  Compile Binary / Container  |     |   Generate Dependency SBOM    |
|  (e.g., Go, Rust, or Docker) |     |   (CycloneDX JSON Format)     |
+------------------------------+     +-------------------------------+
         \                                             /
          ---------------------------------------------
                              |
                              v
+-------------------------------------------------------------+
|            GitLab SLSA Provenance Attestation Engine        |
|  - Generates in-toto attestation JSON statement             |
|  - Cryptographically signs metadata via GitLab OIDC tokens  |
|  - Publishes verified package to GitLab Package Registry    |
+-------------------------------------------------------------+

GitLab has standardized on CycloneDX JSON as its primary SBOM specification.
You can generate CycloneDX SBOMs natively for your dependencies (npm, pip, cargo, go) by integrating standard scanners or using GitLab's built-in Dependency-Scanning template:
stages:
  - test
  - sbom

generate_sbom:
  stage: sbom
  image: alpine:latest
  before_script:
    - apk add --no-cache curl
    # Install Syft (Industry standard open-source SBOM generator)
    - curl -sSfL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/anchore/syft/main/install.sh | sh -s -- -b /usr/local/bin
  script:
    - echo "Generating CycloneDX SBOM for project dependencies..."
    - syft dir:. -o cyclonedx-json=gl-sbom-report.cdx.json
  artifacts:
    paths:
      - gl-sbom-report.cdx.json
    reports:
      cyclonedx: gl-sbom-report.cdx.json # GitLab natively parses this!

reports:cyclonedx is Essential:


By declaring reports:cyclonedx, GitLab automatically ingests the SBOM into your project's Security & Compliance $\rightarrow$ Dependency List dashboard, continuously cross-referencing your packages against the GitLab Advisory Database!
SLSA (Supply-chain Levels for Software Artifacts) provides a vendor-neutral framework to prevent build tampering.
GitLab has built-in native support for generating SLSA provenance metadata for build artifacts. In .gitlab-ci.yml, you declare the artifacts you want to attest:
stages:
  - build
  - release

compile_secure_binary:
  stage: build
  image: golang:1.23-alpine
  script:
    - mkdir -p dist/
    - CGO_ENABLED=0 go build -ldflags="-s -w" -o dist/my-service ./cmd/main.go
    - sha256sum dist/my-service > dist/checksums.txt
  artifacts:
    paths:
      - dist/my-service
      - dist/checksums.txt
    # GitLab automatically generates and attaches SLSA provenance!
    reports:
      slsa_provenance: dist/provenance.json

When this job completes, GitLab’s runner mints an in-toto provenance statement containing:
The exact git commit SHA and repository URL.
The runner environment architecture and pipeline ID.
The SHA-256 hash of the generated binary artifact (dist/my-service).
For Docker images, you can sign both the container image and its attached SBOM using Sigstore / Cosign powered by GitLab's native OIDC JWT tokens:
sign_container_image:
  stage: release
  image:
    name: gcr.io/projectsigstore/cosign:v2.4.0
    entrypoint: [""]
  id_tokens:
    SIGSTORE_ID_TOKEN:
      aud: sigstore
  variables:
    IMAGE_URI: "$CI_REGISTRY_IMAGE:$CI_COMMIT_SHA"
  script:
    - echo "Signing container image with keyless Sigstore OIDC..."
    - cosign login "$CI_REGISTRY" -u "$CI_REGISTRY_USER" -p "$CI_REGISTRY_PASSWORD"

    # 1. Sign container image using ephemeral GitLab OIDC token
    - cosign sign --identity-token "$SIGSTORE_ID_TOKEN" "$IMAGE_URI"

    # 2. Attach CycloneDX SBOM to container image registry
    - cosign attach sbom --sbom gl-sbom-report.cdx.json "$IMAGE_URI"

Consumers can now verify the image before running it in production:
cosign verify \
  --certificate-identity "https://gitlab.com/my-org/my-project//.gitlab-ci.yml@refs/heads/main" \
  --certificate-oidc-issuer "https://gitlab.com" \
  registry.gitlab.com/my-org/my-project:a1b2c3d

Standardize on CycloneDX: Ingest SBOMs directly into GitLab using artifacts:reports:cyclonedx.
Attest Every Binary: Use native SLSA provenance reports to prove artifacts originated from verified source code.
Keyless Signing with OIDC: Combine Sigstore/Cosign with GitLab's id_tokens to eliminate private key management risks.
GitLab Supply Chain Security Documentation: docs.gitlab.com/ee/user/application_security/

Testing Across Everything: Mastering Matrix Builds & Parallelism in GitLab CI/CD
articles.description:
Testing Across Everything: Mastering Matrix Builds & Parallelism in GitLab CI/CD


When maintaining an open-source library, cross-platform CLI tool, or multi-tenant backend, you can never assume that code passing on Node.js 22 or Python 3.12 on Linux will run without errors on Node 18 or Python 3.10 on macOS.
Historically, testing multiple versions in CI meant one of two terrible options:
The Sequential Slow-Down: Running tests for Python 3.10, then 3.11, then 3.12 one after another inside a single job. A 5-minute test suite turns into a 25-minute crawl.
The Copy-Paste YAML Nightmare: Duplicating 40 lines of CI job configuration 6 times with different image tags.
Fortunately, GitLab CI/CD features native Parallel Matrix Builds (parallel: matrix:).
In this practical guide, I will show you how to write clean, concise matrix configurations that fan out across dozens of language versions, database engines, and CPU architectures in parallel.
+-------------------------------------------------------------+
|               Single Job Definition in YAML                 |
|                                                             |
|   parallel:                                                 |
|     matrix:                                                 |
|       - RUNTIME: [3.10, 3.11, 3.12]                         |
|         DATABASE: [postgres, mysql]                         |
+-------------------------------------------------------------+
                              |
                              v (GitLab fans out 6 parallel jobs)
+-------------------------------------------------------------+
|  [Job 1] Python 3.10 + Postgres (Runs on Runner A)         |
|  [Job 2] Python 3.10 + MySQL    (Runs on Runner B)         |
|  [Job 3] Python 3.11 + Postgres (Runs on Runner C)         |
|  [Job 4] Python 3.11 + MySQL    (Runs on Runner D)         |
|  [Job 5] Python 3.12 + Postgres (Runs on Runner E)         |
|  [Job 6] Python 3.12 + MySQL    (Runs on Runner F)         |
|                                                             |
|  * All 6 jobs execute simultaneously! Total time: ~3 mins!  |
+-------------------------------------------------------------+

Here is how to test a Node.js library across LTS releases (18-alpine, 20-alpine, 22-alpine) in parallel:
stages:
  - test

test_node_matrix:
  stage: test
  image: node:$NODE_VERSION
  parallel:
    matrix:
      - NODE_VERSION:
          - "18-alpine"
          - "20-alpine"
          - "22-alpine"
  script:
    - node -v
    - npm ci
    - npm test

In the pipeline graph, GitLab automatically labels the dynamically created jobs:
test_node_matrix: [18-alpine]
test_node_matrix: [20-alpine]
test_node_matrix: [22-alpine]
Each job runs concurrently on available runners, cutting test feedback latency by 66%.
When your backend supports multiple database backends, combine multiple variables into a 2D matrix:
test_backend_grid:
  stage: test
  image: python:$PYTHON_VERSION-slim
  services:
    - name: $DB_IMAGE
      alias: db
  parallel:
    matrix:
      - PYTHON_VERSION: ["3.11", "3.12"]
        DB_IMAGE: ["postgres:16-alpine", "mariadb:11.4"]
  variables:
    POSTGRES_DB: test_db
    POSTGRES_PASSWORD: secretpassword
    MARIADB_DATABASE: test_db
    MARIADB_ROOT_PASSWORD: secretpassword
  script:
    - python -V
    - pip install -r requirements.txt
    - pytest tests/

GitLab computes the Cartesian product ($2 \times 2 = 4$ jobs), provisioning isolated ephemeral database service containers for each permutation.
What if a specific runtime combination is unsupported (e.g., Python 3.10 is incompatible with a modern library requiring Python 3.11+)?
You can define multiple independent matrix arrays within the same block:
test_compatibility:
  stage: test
  image: $BASE_IMAGE
  parallel:
    matrix:
      # Block 1: Linux x86_64 across full stack
      - BASE_IMAGE: ["ubuntu:24.04", "debian:12-slim"]
        ARCH: ["amd64"]
      # Block 2: ARM64 targets (scoped only to Alpine)
      - BASE_IMAGE: ["alpine:3.20"]
        ARCH: ["arm64"]
  script:
    - echo "Compiling binary for $BASE_IMAGE on $ARCH..."

If you don't have multiple language versions, but your test suite has 2,000 slow unit tests, you can use integer test sharding (parallel: N):
shard_tests:
  stage: test
  image: ruby:3.2
  parallel: 4 # Spawns 4 parallel runners: 1/4, 2/4, 3/4, 4/4
  script:
    # Use knapsack or rspec test sharding
    - bundle exec rspec $(bin/split_specs --index $CI_NODE_INDEX --total $CI_NODE_TOTAL)

$CI_NODE_INDEX (e.g. 1) and $CI_NODE_TOTAL (e.g. 4) are injected automatically by GitLab, allowing your test runner to slice the test directory evenly across runners.
Eliminate Duplicated YAML: Let GitLab generate Cartesian product permutations dynamically using parallel: matrix:.
True Concurrent Feedback: Multi-version validation finishes in the time of a single run.
Combine with Caching: Ensure dependency caches are partitioned by runtime version (key: "$CI_JOB_NAME") to prevent cross-version cache poisoning.
GitLab CI/CD Matrix Documentation: docs.gitlab.com/ee/ci/yaml/#parallelmatrix

articles.title: Architecting Real-Time Streaming in DevOps: Server-Sent Events, WebSockets & MCP in GitLab
articles.description:
Architecting Real-Time Streaming in DevOps: Server-Sent Events, WebSockets & MCP in GitLab


Traditional web applications rely on standard request-response HTTP cycles. You submit a form or fetch a list of items, and the server returns a complete payload.
However, in modern DevOps platforms and AI systems like GitLab, static HTTP falls short:
Live CI/CD Terminal Output: Developers need to watch compiler logs and test outputs stream line-by-line in real time.
AI Code Suggestions & Duo Chat: When an LLM generates a 200-line refactor, waiting 15 seconds for the entire response to buffer feels painfully sluggish compared to streaming tokens instantaneously as they are computed.
Model Context Protocol (MCP): Connecting autonomous AI agents (such as Cline, Cursor, or Antigravity) to GitLab requires persistent bidirectional or event-driven streaming transports like Server-Sent Events (SSE) and stdio.
In this architecture guide, we will unpack how real-time streaming works across GitLab’s core infrastructure, comparing WebSockets, Server-Sent Events (SSE), and MCP streaming transports, and show how to implement a high-throughput SSE streaming service.
+-------------------------------------------------------------+
|                      WEBSOCKETS (Full-Duplex)               |
|                                                             |
|   Client  <====== Bidirectional TCP Upgrade (ws://) ======> |
|   - Best for: Interactive web terminal consoles (xterm.js). |
|   - Drawback: Complex proxy buffering, corporate firewalls. |
+-------------------------------------------------------------+

                              vs.

+-------------------------------------------------------------+
|                SERVER-SENT EVENTS / SSE (Half-Duplex)       |
|                                                             |
|   Client  <--- Single HTTP/2 Stream (text/event-stream) --- |
|   - Best for: GitLab Duo Chat token streaming, CI logs.     |
|   - Advantage: Native browser reconnects, simple HTTP/2.    |
+-------------------------------------------------------------+

                              vs.

+-------------------------------------------------------------+
|              MODEL CONTEXT PROTOCOL (MCP stdio / SSE)       |
|                                                             |
|   Agent  <=== JSON-RPC 2.0 Packets over stdio or SSE ===>   |
|   - Best for: Autonomous AI coding agents querying GitLab.  |
|   - Advantage: Standardized capability negotiation.         |
+-------------------------------------------------------------+

When building streaming services for GitLab Duo or custom developer bots, Server-Sent Events (SSE) is almost always the superior choice over WebSockets:
It runs over standard HTTP/1.1 or HTTP/2 (Content-Type: text/event-stream).
Standard HTTP load balancers (NGINX, Cloudflare, Traefik) proxy it seamlessly without special upgrade handshakes.
Native browser support (EventSource) handles automatic exponential backoff reconnection out of the box.
import asyncio
from fastapi import FastAPI
from fastapi.responses import StreamingResponse

app = FastAPI()

async def generate_token_stream(prompt: str):
    """Simulates real-time token generation from an AI model engine."""
    tokens = [
        "def ", "calculate_metrics", "(data: ", "list):", "\n",
        "    # Fast vector aggregation\n",
        "    return ", "sum(data) ", "/ ", "len(data)\n"
    ]

    for token in tokens:
        # Format payload strictly adhering to the SSE standard: `data: <content>\n\n`
        yield f"data: {token}\n\n"
        await asyncio.sleep(0.04) # Simulate 40ms token generation interval

@app.post("/v1/stream-suggestions")
async def stream_suggestions(payload: dict):
    prompt = payload.get("prompt", "")
    return StreamingResponse(
        generate_token_stream(prompt),
        media_type="text/event-stream",
        headers={
            "Cache-Control": "no-cache",
            "Connection": "keep-alive",
            "X-Accel-Buffering": "no" # Prevents NGINX from buffering chunked output!
        }
    )

Crucial Production Gotcha: The X-Accel-Buffering: no header tells reverse proxies like NGINX not to buffer responses. Without this header, NGINX will buffer 4KB of output before sending any packets, completely breaking the real-time streaming illusion!
In GitLab Core (where we contributed MR !260212 for MCP resources), the Model Context Protocol introduces two standard streaming transports:
stdio (Local Process Pipe):
When running locally inside an IDE or terminal, the AI client spawns the GitLab MCP server as a sub-process and streams newline-delimited JSON-RPC messages over standard input and output.
Zero networking overhead, sub-millisecond local latency.
SSE Transport (Remote Web Services):
For remote GitLab instances, the client opens a GET request to an /sse endpoint to receive server-sent events.
The server replies with an active session ID and endpoint URI, allowing the client to POST JSON-RPC commands while receiving real-time responses over the persistent SSE pipe.
Connecting a frontend web dashboard to an SSE stream in modern web applications requires minimal boilerplate:
async function fetchStreamingSuggestion(prompt: string, onToken: (text: string) => void) {
  const response = await fetch('/v1/stream-suggestions', {
    method: 'POST',
    headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' },
    body: JSON.stringify({ prompt })
  });

  const reader = response.body?.getReader();
  const decoder = new TextDecoder('utf-8');

  if (!reader) return;

  while (true) {
    const { done, value } = await reader.read();
    if (done) break;

    const chunk = decoder.decode(value, { stream: true });
    const lines = chunk.split('\n');

    for (const line of lines) {
      if (line.startsWith('data: ')) {
        const token = line.replace('data: ', '');
        onToken(token);
      }
    }
  }
}

Prefer SSE for LLMs & Logs: Server-Sent Events provide native HTTP caching, reconnection, and simplicity compared to full-duplex WebSockets.
Disable Reverse Proxy Buffering: Always set X-Accel-Buffering: no on your streaming endpoints to prevent NGINX or Traefik from delaying tokens.
Embrace Open Protocol Standards: Standardized protocols like MCP ensure your streaming services are instantly compatible with any AI client across the industry.

articles.title: Zero-Secret Pipelines: Hardening GitLab CI/CD with OIDC & HashiCorp Vault
articles.description:
Zero-Secret Pipelines: Hardening GitLab CI/CD with OIDC & HashiCorp Vault


Every security team's worst nightmare begins with a developer committing a secret to Git, or an attacker compromising a project's CI/CD variable settings.
For years, connecting GitLab CI/CD to external infrastructure (AWS, Google Cloud, Azure, or internal databases) meant creating static, long-lived credentials:
An AWS IAM Access Key and Secret Key pasted into GitLab CI variables.
A database password stored in plaintext inside runner environments.
Tokens that rarely get rotated and live indefinitely.
If a rogue merge request or malicious dependency executes env inside a build script, your entire cloud infrastructure is compromised.
The modern industry gold standard for CI/CD security is Zero Stored Secrets using OpenID Connect (OIDC).
In this practical guide, I will show you how to configure GitLab CI/CD’s native id_tokens to dynamically authenticate against HashiCorp Vault or cloud providers, minting short-lived (15-minute) credentials on demand with zero static secrets stored in GitLab.
+-------------------------------------------------------------+
|                     TRADITIONAL STATIC MODEL                |
|                                                             |
|  GitLab CI Runner reads:                                    |
|  $AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID = "AKIA..." (Static, never rotated)     |
|  $AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY = "wJal..." (Massive leak risk!)    |
+-------------------------------------------------------------+

                              vs.

+-------------------------------------------------------------+
|                  ZERO-SECRET OIDC FEDERATION                |
|                                                             |
|  1. GitLab Runner generates cryptographically signed JWT    |
|     token (`id_tokens: GITLAB_OIDC_TOKEN`)                  |
|  2. Token contains claims: project_id, branch, user_login  |
|  3. HashiCorp Vault / Cloud IAM verifies GitLab's OIDC pubkey|
|  4. Vault issues temporary 15-minute token scoped to branch |
|  5. Zero credentials stored in GitLab repository settings!  |
+-------------------------------------------------------------+

Inside your HashiCorp Vault cluster, enable the JWT/OIDC authentication engine and establish trust with GitLab’s public identity provider:
# 1. Enable the JWT auth method
vault auth enable jwt

# 2. Configure Vault to trust GitLab's OpenID Connect issuer
vault write auth/jwt/config \
    oidc_discovery_url="https://gitlab.com" \
    bound_issuer="https://gitlab.com"

Next, define a Vault role that restricts access based on strict GitLab JWT claims (e.g., only commits on the protected main branch of project my-org/core-infra):
vault write auth/jwt/role/gitlab-production-deployer \
    role_type="jwt" \
    bound_audiences="https://vault.mycompany.com" \
    user_claim="user_email" \
    bound_claims_type="glob" \
    bound_claims='{
      "project_path": "my-org/core-infra",
      "ref": "main",
      "ref_type": "branch"
    }' \
    policies="production-database-read" \
    ttl="15m"

If an attacker tries to run a pipeline from an unapproved fork or feature branch, Vault automatically rejects the token!
.gitlab-ci.yml


In your GitLab CI configuration, declare id_tokens with an audience matching your Vault configuration. GitLab automatically signs this JSON Web Token using its private key:
stages:
  - deploy

deploy_production:
  stage: deploy
  image: hashicorp/vault:latest
  environment: production
  id_tokens:
    # GitLab generates a cryptographically signed OIDC JWT
    VAULT_ID_TOKEN:
      aud: https://vault.mycompany.com
  variables:
    VAULT_ADDR: "https://vault.mycompany.com:8200"
  rules:
    - if: $CI_COMMIT_BRANCH == "main"
  script:
    - |
      echo "Authenticating against HashiCorp Vault with ephemeral OIDC JWT..."

      # 1. Exchange the GitLab OIDC token for a 15-minute Vault Client Token
      VAULT_AUTH_RESPONSE=$(vault write -format=json auth/jwt/login \
        role="gitlab-production-deployer" \
        jwt="$VAULT_ID_TOKEN")

      export VAULT_TOKEN=$(echo $VAULT_AUTH_RESPONSE | jq -r '.auth.client_token')

      # 2. Fetch the dynamic database secret from Vault
      DB_SECRET=$(vault kv get -format=json secret/production/database)
      DB_PASSWORD=$(echo $DB_SECRET | jq -r '.data.data.password')

      echo "Executing deployment with ephemeral secret..."
      ./scripts/deploy.sh --db-pass "$DB_PASSWORD"

GitLab embeds rich contextual metadata directly into every OIDC token:



JWT Claim
Example Value
Security Use Case




iss
https://gitlab.com
Verifies the token originated from GitLab.


project_path
my-org/core-infra
Restricts secrets to exact repository paths.


ref
main
Ensures production secrets never leak to feature branches.


environment
production
Binds access to protected GitLab environments.


user_login
hrlpavan
Enforces identity auditing for human triggers.


ci_config_sha
a1b2c3d4...
Pins access to specific audited CI configurations.



Zero Secret Leakage: Even if a developer accidentally runs printenv or prints build artifacts, there are no permanent AWS or database passwords stored in GitLab.
Deterministic Expiration: Ephemeral tokens expire automatically after 15 minutes, neutralizing replay attacks.
No Rotation Ceremonies: Security teams never have to schedule quarterly downtime to rotate static cloud passwords.
Complete IAM Auditability: Cloud and Vault access logs record the exact GitLab project, user, and commit SHA responsible for every request.

articles.title: GitLab Duo vs. GitHub Copilot: An Architectural Deep-Dive from an Open-Source Contributor
articles.description:
GitLab Duo vs. GitHub Copilot: An Architectural Deep-Dive from an Open-Source Contributor


As artificial intelligence becomes an indispensable companion in every developer's daily workflow, two enterprise giants dominate the AI-assisted DevOps landscape: GitHub Copilot and GitLab Duo.
Most comparison articles online stay on the surface: "Which one writes better JavaScript functions?" or "Which tool has faster autocomplete in VS Code?"
As an active contributor who has contributed code to both GitLab Core (implementing Model Context Protocol resources in MR !260212) and the GitLab AI Gateway (MR !7251), I wanted to offer a much deeper, architectural evaluation.
How do these two platforms actually work under the hood? How do they handle model lifecycles, data privacy, enterprise compliance, and open protocols like MCP?
Here is the architectural comparison.
+-------------------------------------------------------------+
|                      GITHUB COPILOT                         |
|                                                             |
|   Client IDE  <== (Proprietary Tunnel) ==>  Azure OpenAI    |
|   - Closed proprietary API routes                           |
|   - Hard-locked to Microsoft Azure infrastructure           |
|   - Enterprise cannot inspect prompt construction           |
+-------------------------------------------------------------+

                              vs.

+-------------------------------------------------------------+
|                        GITLAB DUO                           |
|                                                             |
|   Client IDE  --->  GitLab Core  --->  GitLab AI Gateway    |
|                                                 |           |
|                                         +-------+-------+   |
|                                         |       |       |   |
|                                       Vertex  Claude  Self- |
|                                         AI     3.7   Hosted |
|   - Open source, standalone AI Gateway (FastAPI/Python)     |
|   - Model-agnostic routing (Google, Anthropic, AWS, Local)  |
|   - Full code transparency across prompt compiler logic     |
+-------------------------------------------------------------+

GitHub Copilot: Deeply coupled to the Microsoft Azure ecosystem and OpenAI models (GPT-4o, o1, o3-mini). You cannot self-host the backend or inspect how prompts are tokenized and assembled.
GitLab Duo: Built on the open-source GitLab AI Gateway (gitlab-org/modelops/.../ai-assist). The prompt templates, model routing tables (models.yml), and unit primitives are completely public and inspectable by any developer on GitLab.
When building complex software, one model does not fit all tasks:
Fast autocomplete requires sub-100ms lightweight models.
Deep architectural refactoring requires multi-turn reasoning and 1M+ context windows.



Feature
GitHub Copilot
GitLab Duo




Model Selection
GPT-4o, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, o1 (Closed preview)
Claude 3.7/3.5 Sonnet, Gemini 4 Argon, Gemini 1.5 Pro, Vertex AI


Self-Hosted LLMs
No (Cloud-only)
Yes (Bring Your Own Model via vLLM / Ollama)


Context Window Size
~8K – 32K active prompt context
Up to 1,000,000 tokens (Gemini 4 Argon / 1.5 Pro)


Air-Gapped Deployment
No
Yes (GitLab Self-Managed with Local GPUs)



By incorporating frontier models like Google's Gemini with 1,000,000-token context windows, GitLab Duo can ingest entire repositories, architecture specs, and multi-file dependency trees simultaneously during code reviews.
This is where the two ecosystems diverge most dramatically.
While Copilot relies on proprietary GitHub Extensions and bespoke Copilot Agents:
GitLab Core has embraced the Model Context Protocol (MCP) as an open standard.
Any open-source AI agent (such as Cline, Cursor, Claude Desktop, or Antigravity) can connect directly to GitLab's MCP server endpoints (resources/list, resources/templates/list) via standard JSON-RPC.




{
  "jsonrpc": "2.0",
  "method": "resources/read",
  "params": {
    "uri": "gitlab://projects/123/issues/456"
  }
}

This prevents vendor lock-in. You aren't restricted to a single editor extension; your entire AI toolkit can interact with your GitLab codebase over open, standardized protocols.
Where GitLab Duo truly shines is its integration across the broader software development lifecycle:
Vulnerability Explanation & Auto-Remediation:


When a SAST or Secret Detection pipeline flags a SQL injection in GitLab, Duo can explain the vulnerability in plain English and generate an automated Merge Request patch with one click.
Root Cause Analysis in CI/CD:


If a build job or test fails in .gitlab-ci.yml, clicking "Root Cause Analysis" asks Duo to parse the failed job logs, correlate them with recent git commits, and suggest the exact fix.
Value Stream Analytics:


Duo provides AI-driven forecasting for deployment frequency and code review turnaround bottlenecks across your organization.
Copilot excels inside the code editor itself, but GitLab Duo is woven deeply into the entire DevOps pipeline.
For enterprise legal and security teams, data sovereignty is non-negotiable:
GitLab Privacy Guarantee: Code and prompts sent to GitLab Duo are never used to train foundational AI models. Telemetry is stripped of customer identifiers, and self-hosted instances can run completely air-gapped without making outbound internet calls.
Auditable Prompts: Because the AI Gateway code is public, compliance teams can audit the exact prompts, system instructions, and redaction rules before approving deployment.
Your team's workflow is 100% centralized inside VS Code and GitHub.com.
You primarily want inline autocomplete and basic chat without needing to customize model backends.
Your organization is already all-in on the Microsoft Azure / OpenAI ecosystem.
You operate a modern DevSecOps pipeline and want AI assistance on CI/CD failures, vulnerability patches, and code reviews.

Hypit: Automação e criação de vídeos com agentes de IA
articles.description:
O que é


O Hypit é um sistema de código aberto que fornece a agentes de inteligência artificial, como Claude Code e Codex, uma linguagem e estrutura para a criação e edição de vídeos. A ferramenta permite estruturar fluxos de trabalho completos de vídeo, incluindo imagens, legendas, B-rolls e efeitos visuais, todos ancorados diretamente em palavras em vez de marcações de tempo em segundos.
A criação pode começar a partir da clonagem do fluxo de um vídeo de referência, do uso de modelos predefinidos ou apenas descrevendo o resultado desejado para que o agente escreva o projeto do zero. Além disso, os modelos de geração são opcionais: o sistema consegue compilar legendas, gráficos em movimento e visuais renderizados por código sem acionar modelos pagos.
O projeto é voltado para desenvolvedores, editores e criadores que utilizam agentes de codificação e desejam automatizar a produção de conteúdo audiovisual. É adequado para quem busca gerar múltiplas variações de um vídeo de forma automatizada ou integrar scripts de renderização gráfica diretamente no processo de criação.
O Hypit é gratuito e funciona com Node.js (versão 22.15 ou superior) e gerenciadores como pnpm. Para instalar a habilidade no seu ambiente de agente, execute o comando:
npx skills add hypit-ai/hypit -g
Na primeira utilização, o agente verifica a presença do executável e ajuda a preparar o ambiente. É possível utilizar o serviço hospedado HypiHub ou conectar APIs próprias e modelos locais fornecendo a documentação ao agente.
npx skills add hypit-ai/hypit -g

The Real Cost of Running LLMs On-Premise (It's Not What You Think)
articles.description:
GPU bills, hallucinations, and the dream of free AI inference. A full TCO breakdown including the 40 hours of debugging nobody talks about.
#localai#cost#gpu
Sarah, an engineering director at a mid-size logistics firm, pulled the trigger on a local GPU after her cloud inference bill hit $8,000 in a single month. The hardware arrived on a Tuesday. By Friday she had CUDA working. By week three she had her first pipeline running.
Modest monthly power. That was the surprise after the first full month. A local GPU running 24/7, serving inference from several automation workflows simultaneously — including one that fires on a schedule, makes dozens of model calls per run, and never sleeps. A hundred thousand tokens a day, minimum. The power line item was modest — not free, but a fraction of equivalent cloud API spend for the same volume.
Monthly power cost — GPU + system 24/7Modest / moEst. daily drawLow–mid hundreds of wattsGPU + host · 24/7 inference loadUptime today24/7GPU inference running since midnight...
I stared at that number for longer than I should have, because it's genuinely disorienting. One heavy afternoon on a frontier cloud API at that request volume costs more. And yet — and this is the part the "free local inference" crowd skips — the power bill is not the real number. Not even close. The real number is harder to face.
Vague claims about "saving money on API costs" are how self-hosted projects lie to themselves. Here are my actual numbers across the first three months.

$58–73per month · incl. hardware amortizationLocal GPU · 14B models · 100k+ tokens/day
$180–240per month · frontier API model at this volumeest. ~500k tokens/day · input + outputFOR EQUIVALENT INFERENCE VOLUME (EST. ~500K TOKENS/DAY)



Cost Item
Amount
Notes




GPU (hardware)
Mid-range card
Amortized over 24 months


Host upgrade (additional RAM)
One-time kit
Amortized over 24 months


Electricity (GPU + system at 24/7)
Modest monthly
Low–mid hundreds of watts total draw


Total monthly run cost
~$58–73/mo
Including hardware amortization


Cloud API equivalent (my volume)
$180–240/mo
frontier API model at my request volume + context


Net monthly savings
$107–180/mo
After breakeven in month 4



The math works — but only with a specific usage profile: high volume, repetitive tasks (job classification, extraction, structured output), privacy-sensitive data that cannot leave the network, and willingness to accept "very good" instead of "state of the art." Below 100 calls/day, the API is cheaper once you count your time honestly.
When On-Prem Makes Sense FinanciallyHigh-volume repetitive inference (hundreds of calls per day), pipelines where API costs compound daily, or any workflow involving data you will not send to a third party. Economic breakeven: roughly 3–4 months for a $500–600 GPU versus $180–240/month equivalent cloud cost. Below that volume threshold, API wins — especially when you count setup hours.

Here is what "free local inference" actually costs: forty hours of my life in the first three months that had nothing to do with building AI systems.
CUDA driver conflict after a host OS kernel update — four hours. Ollama hostname resolution breaking after a Docker network change — six hours. A model producing silently corrupted JSON output that turned out to be a GPU memory allocation bug — eight hours. GPU sitting at 60% utilization during a batch job for reasons I still can't fully explain — three hours of profiling. Miscellaneous config drift, model redownloads, and Ollama version pinning — the rest.
What did those forty hours teach me that I wouldn't have learned from an API? Genuinely: how inference engines allocate GPU memory under concurrent load, how Docker networking interacts with GPU passthrough on a self-hosted NAS, how context window size affects system RAM (not just GPU memory) in ways the benchmarks don't show. That knowledge is now part of how I design systems. It was not free. It was paid for in the most expensive currency there is.
The question is not whether you'll pay that cost — you will. The question is whether you're going in with eyes open. A cloud API call costs money the moment you make it. A local inference call costs time, invisibly, spread across months of ownership. Both are real. Only one shows up on a bill.
The Bottleneck Isn't Where You Think
Every local LLM guide focuses on GPU memory — and it matters. But I hit a hard wall at modest system RAM long before I hit the GPU memory ceiling. Large context windows were causing the host OS to page aggressively, slowing inference to a crawl that negated every advantage of having the GPU. The fix wasn't a better GPU. It was upgrading system RAM — a kit that made more difference to real-world throughput than any model optimization I tried. If you're running 14B+ models with long contexts: spec your system RAM like it matters, because it does.
Volume is a spreadsheet argument. Privacy is a different kind of argument — and it's the one that actually drove my decision.
Consider what my pipelines process. Document ingestion workflows: structured records, version history, every revision of generated output. Form automation pipelines: contact details, preference data, personal statements. A daily reflection system: what I'm worried about, what I'm working toward, what I think about people I work with. Infrastructure health monitoring: which services are running, what state they're in, the shape of the whole system.
None of that leaves this building. Not one token of it goes to OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, or any cloud provider. It runs on a GPU sitting three feet from me, processed by a model that has no network access, no logging to anyone else's servers, no terms of service that give a corporation rights to my career data. That's not paranoia. That's a deliberate architecture decision about which data I'm comfortable externalizing and which I'm not.
Most "local LLM" posts frame privacy as a bonus feature — nice to have, not necessary. I'd invert that. Once you systematically audit which of your workflows process personal data, you realize how much of it you've been casually sending to third-party infrastructure. Local inference doesn't just change the cost equation. It changes what you're willing to build.
I use frontier cloud APIs and Claude without apology for specific things, despite having capable local GPU inference available:

Frontier-level reasoning — architectural decisions, complex multi-step debugging, writing that needs to be genuinely good
One-off tasks where local setup overhead exceeds the cost of just making an API call
Anything where a wrong answer has real consequences and 14B capability isn't enough
Tasks involving public data where privacy isn't a factor and quality matters most
The 14B capability ceiling is real. Local models are excellent at classification, extraction, structured output, and pattern-matched code completion. They are unreliable at nuanced judgment and complex reasoning chains. Know the ceiling. Route accordingly. Hybrid is not a compromise — it's correct architecture.
The Only Question That Matters Will I run this model 100+ times per day, every day, for the next 12 months — on data I'd rather not send to a cloud API?
If yes: buy the GPU. The economics and the privacy case both hold. If no: the API is cheaper, faster to start with, and zero maintenance overhead. There's no shame in that answer. The mistake is buying hardware for occasional use and pretending the 40 hours of infrastructure work doesn't count as cost.
Modest monthly power. Hardware amortizes cleanly. The RAM upgrade was worth every dollar. The forty hours of debugging were paid forward — that knowledge is now structural. And the model that runs my automation pipelines, watches my infrastructure, and handles my daily reflections is sitting three feet from me, thinking on my hardware, sending nothing anywhere.
That's the real cost. And it's worth it — if you go in knowing what you're actually buying.

Your move: Before you buy anything, pull up your cloud API billing for the last three months. Count total tokens, sum the cost, and divide by 30. If the monthly number is above the amortized cost of a mid-range GPU (roughly $25–30/month over 24 months), the economics deserve a spreadsheet. If it's below, keep paying the API bill — your time is worth more than the savings. Either way, run one pipeline on local inference, not to save money, but to learn what you don't know yet.
"Forty hours of CUDA debugging is not a tax. It's tuition. But you should know which one you're paying before you buy the GPU."
Stay with us · poll
As you weigh the pros and cons of running large language models on-premise versus in the cloud, what factors do you consider most important? Share your thoughts below!
No account needed — pick a take, then keep reading. We rotate these prompts so each piece feels like a conversation, not a clone.
Ayraix.com publisher analysis
When considering the total cost of ownership (TCO) for running large language models (LLMs) on-premise versus in the cloud, it's easy to get caught up in the allure of lower power bills. However, as Sarah's experience with her local GPU setup demonstrates, the true costs extend far beyond just electricity. The upfront investment in hardware and ongoing maintenance can quickly add up, making the decision between on-premise and cloud hosting a nuanced one.
While on-premise solutions offer control and potentially lower operational costs for high-volume inference tasks, they require careful consideration of the initial financial outlay and long-term sustainability. Cloud services, although more expensive in terms of API costs, often provide greater flexibility and scalability, which can be invaluable for businesses with fluctuating workloads.
