PwnEscape: Guest-to-Host KVM Escape and Host Memory Leak via Linux Checksum Processing (CVE-2026-99999)
articles.description:
1. Basic Information




Article Name: PwnEscape: Guest-to-Host KVM Escape (CVE-2026-99999)
Source: pwn.ai / PWNAI Research, Paulos Yibelo
Publication Date: October 15, 2026 (Estimated based on the article record creation date. The official publication date and time are not set.)
Updated Date: October 18, 2026, 11:20 JST (Original metadata)
Source URL: pwn.ai: PwnEscape


Related Information Sources: Linux CNA: CVE-2026-99999 Official Record, Linux Fix Commit 6785011f8b16, Vercel: Findings from the 1 Million Dollar Vercel Sandbox Challenge, Red Hat: CVE-2026-99999, Amazon Linux: CVE-2026-99999, Linux Kernel Documentation: Checksum Offloads, MITRE ATT&CK: Escape to Host


Related Malware / Attack Groups: None publicly disclosed
Related CVE: CVE-2026-99999
Related Products: Linux kernel IPv4 processing, virtio-net / TUN/TAP, KVM, Firecracker, Vercel Sandbox
Severity: Critical
The Linux CNA rated CVSS v3.1 at 9.3. The impact crosses the isolation boundary between the guest and the host, with production memory leaks and host code execution in researcher-owned environments reported. Red Hat assigned a score of 8.8; these scores come from different rating authorities.
A Linux flaw allows guest-provided checksum metadata to overwrite validated IPv4 headers. Production memory leaks and host code execution in a research environment have been reported, requiring remediation on the host kernel side.
The following are sequential phases described by pwn.ai. Additional memory manipulation is required to progress from the first half (memory leak) to the second half (host execution). This does not mean the entire attack can be reproduced using only the first part of the disclosure.



Phase
Verified Environment
Key Technical Actions
Confirmed Impact Scope




Phase 1
Vercel production sandbox and researcher-owned environments
Used guest-controlled checksum metadata on packets marked CHECKSUM_PARTIAL to overwrite validated IPv4 headers (the header length indicated by IHL changed from 20 to 60 bytes in the research example)
Demonstrated host memory leaks in production. In the researcher's controlled experiment, sent 32 bytes beyond valid 28-byte linear data as IPv4 options. No reports of customer data acquisition


Phase 2 (pwn.ai demonstration)
Researcher-owned KVM test environment only
Used host memory observations and allocation control to achieve selected 64-byte writes to host kernel memory and execute a helper program with root privileges
Returned host-generated markers to the guest across four independent cold boots (detailed procedures not disclosed in Part 1; host code execution not confirmed in the Vercel production environment)



An attacker within the guest passes transmitted frames and crafted virtio-net checksum metadata to the host virtual network path.
The host validates the IPv4 header while retaining the checksum metadata and CHECKSUM_PARTIAL state in sk_buff, proceeding to subsequent output and fragmentation processing.
Delayed checksum calculation writes the result back to the validated IPv4 header. In the research example, the IPv4 header length indicated by IHL changed from 20 to 60 bytes.
Fragmentation processing trusts the modified length, copying beyond the logical 28 bytes of linear data. In the research example, the 32-byte difference was sent externally as IPv4 options.
Using host memory observations and allocation control from Phase 1, the researcher demonstrated selected 64-byte writes to host kernel memory in their own KVM test environment.
They then reported completing a series of steps to execute a helper program with host root privileges, returning a host-generated verification marker to the guest across four independent cold boots.
Details from writing to execution are not disclosed in Part 1. It cannot be determined that arbitrary code execution automatically succeeds based solely on a 32-byte leak.
These 32 bytes are host memory outside the valid linear data of sk_buff. This does not necessarily mean a read beyond the physical allocation region itself. Delayed checksum writing is a standard Linux feature, but the flaw lies in allowing a position that overlaps with the validated header. Researcher's Description, Checksum Specifications
The attacker executes code within an untrusted guest VM and controls the virtual NIC checksum metadata passed to the host. This is distinct from paths that simply send regular IP packets from the internet.
In the Linux CNA microVM scenario, host credentials, privileges, or direct access to /dev/net/tun are unnecessary. The VMM passes guest output to the existing TAP path.
The modified packet processing and ultimate impact occur on the host Linux kernel side. Verify any operations and privileges required on the guest side, including whether the configuration allows manipulating the virtual NIC.
Users: For production memory leaks, Vercel explains that host memory-derived byte sequences were mixed into guest transmitted packets. They state there were no reports of access to customer files, secrets, or application data.
Administrators: The host-crash test showed that all sandboxes on the same host would stop together. The crash and code-execution demonstrations took place on researcher-owned machines.
Administrators: Inference: If it is only a memory leak, there may be no clear anomalies in user screens or standard application logs.
The host runs an unpatched Linux kernel, and the configuration allows malicious guest-provided checksum metadata to reach host IPv4 processing.
Reaching relevant processing steps, such as fragmentation, while able to write checksum results into the validated IPv4 header.
Progression to host execution requires additional conditions, such as the allocation control used in the research. The published leak description alone is insufficient to determine all conditions.
Update the host to a patched kernel. Initial stable patch versions indicated by the Linux CNA are 5.10.272, 5.15.223, 6.1.190, 6.6.159, 6.12.113, 6.18.57, 7.2.11, and mainline 7.3-rc7.
Fix commit 6785011f8b16 checks whether csum_start is at or beyond the end of the IPv4 header across five IPv4 checksum completion routines, rejecting invalid data.
This patch is a defense-in-depth measure to prevent IPv4 header overwriting and does not guarantee overall virtio input validation or correct TCP/UDP checksum positions.
Verify distribution patch versions, backports, and application to running kernels. Updating only the guest kernel cannot fix the vulnerability on the host side.
As of the check on October 18, 2026, Amazon Linux lists the affected kernel packages as Pending Fix. The availability of an upstream patch differs from availability and deployment status across products. Red Hat also has not provided general mitigation measures that can be applied.
References include Linux CNA Fixed Versions, Upstream Fix Diff, Amazon Linux Availability, and Red Hat Mitigation Description.
Host memory confidentiality is compromised. Vercel acknowledged proof of leaks in production sandboxes but did not confirm the acquisition of specific customer data.
In researcher-owned KVM and Firecracker environments, host crashes and code execution with administrator privileges were demonstrated, according to Vercel.
Inference: If the host crashes, co-located workloads are also affected. Cross-tenant compromise or credential theft after host control are potential impacts and are not treated as confirmed damage in this incident.
Email: No email-origin or email log indicators specific to this issue have been published.
Proxy / SWG / DNS: Inference: Standard proxy and DNS logs do not expose packet IHL values or the checksum metadata held in the kernel. Destination records remain auxiliary information.
Endpoint / EDR: Inference: Where host audit or EDR records are available, they can help investigate suspicious root processes or persistence outside isolation boundaries. Kernel-level memory leaks do not necessarily trigger process creation.
Endpoint / EDR: Inference: Host kernel logs and crash dumps help investigate the cause of crashes, but a crash alone does not prove successful code execution.
Identity / IdP: The entry point for this issue is not an authentication service. Since paths not requiring host credentials exist, IdP logs alone cannot track attempts.
SaaS / Cloud: Inference: Correlate VM creation and execution entities, guest and host placement, and management records of host reboots and failures. Managed services require provider-side records and investigations.
Network: The research used transmitted packet observation and independent application-side reception confirmation to substantiate the leak from the host.
Network: Inference: Packet records mapping virtual NIC entry points to host transmission outputs help investigate alterations. However, checksum metadata is separate from the packet payload, and external packet captures alone cannot reconstruct all conditions.
Information theft or session compromise confirmed: Vercel states that host memory leaks were demonstrated in production sandboxes. pwn.ai confirmed a 32-byte leak in its controlled experiments. Vercel said that no reports showed access to customer files, secrets, or application data.
Scope: Demonstration of production host memory leaks and 32-byte disclosures in controlled experiments in a researcher-owned environment. Distinct from actual damage by malicious third parties.
Subsequent compromise confirmed: pwn.ai reported host kernel writes and root-privileged helper program execution in an owned KVM environment, and Vercel described administrator-privileged code execution in owned KVM and Firecracker environments. This does not mean host code execution was confirmed in Vercel production.
Scope: Limited to researcher-owned test environments.
The distinction is between Vercel's demonstration scope and pwn.ai's demonstration in owned environments.
Leaks require evidence that transmitted values are host memory rather than guest-derived data, and host execution requires evidence of execution outside isolation. Markers from public research are validation tools used by researchers, not IOCs present in your organization's environment.
Starting Point for Investigation: Start investigations based on unpatched hosts running untrusted VMs, unexplained host crashes, execution outside isolation, and mismatches in transmitted IPv4 headers.
Initial Verification: Check the host's running kernel, vendor patch application status, virtual NIC and TUN/TAP paths, and guests/execution entities placed on the target host.
Endpoints and Hosts: Preserve host kernel logs, crash dumps, audit/EDR records, and process/persistence records for the target timeframe. Do not retransmit attack packets in your organization's production environment.
Authentication and Cloud: Cross-reference cloud-side VM creators, placement and migration history, and management operations. If direct host investigation is not possible, coordinate with providers regarding investigation scope and patching status.
Subsequent Actions: If execution outside isolation is confirmed on the host, expand the investigation to look for access to other workloads, credential use, and outbound data transfers. These are not publicly confirmed damages of this incident.
Containment: Inference: Isolate suspicious guests and hosts, and halt the placement of new untrusted workloads. Plan updates, reboots, and relocations based on service impact and evidence preservation, verifying operation on patched hosts.
Determination Categories: Assess vulnerable configuration presence, exploit attempts, host memory leaks, host crashes, host code execution, and cross-tenant access separately. Do not treat crashes or IHL anomalies alone as a successful VM escape.
Single Events: Inference: Unusual IPv4 options or host kernel anomalies serve as investigation triggers, but cannot be used alone for specific detection or confirming leaks.
Time-Series Correlation: Inference: Correlate guest transmission records, host transmission packets, simultaneous kernel failures, and process execution outside isolation using host-guest mapping relationships.
Hunting: Inference: Prioritize inventorying unpatched host kernels and co-located untrusted VMs. Exclude normal IPv4 option usage and legitimate host management operations.
Log Gaps and Limitations: Standard DNS, proxy, and IdP logs do not record csum_start or csum_offset. Public materials contain no completed detection signatures or event IDs specific to this issue, and monitoring cannot replace patching.
Priority Countermeasures: Prioritize patching the host kernel and verify patch availability and deployment across products.
Priority Countermeasures: Inference: Placement restrictions or reducing guest privileges until patched are auxiliary measures to reduce reachability, but are not universally effective workarounds. The presence of a virtualization boundary alone is not a reason to trust the host's network processing.
pwn.ai reported a Linux flaw where guest-derived checksum metadata overwrites validated IPv4 headers. The flawed implementation is in host network processing, not KVM itself.
Vercel confirmed host memory leaks in production sandboxes and stated that crashes and code execution were demonstrated in researcher-owned KVM and Firecracker environments. They noted no reports of customer data acquisition.
The leak volume in pwn.ai's controlled experiments is 32 bytes. The series of steps leading to host execution successfully completed four independent cold boots in an owned KVM environment.
Linux fix commit 6785011f8b16 validates the start position before completing IPv4 checksums. This fix does not mean input validation is complete overall.
The Linux CNA rated CVSS v3.1 at 9.3, recording stable patch levels as 5.10.272, 5.15.223, 6.1.190, 6.6.159, 6.12.113, 6.18.57, 7.2.11, and mainline 7.3-rc7.
Even if untrusted code is isolated in a VM, flaws in how the host interprets virtual device information can lead to attacks that cross isolation boundaries.
Guest-internal logs and standard communication logs alone are insufficient to determine host memory leaks or host execution. Operations require managing host-side patches and maintaining host-guest mapping relationships.
No additional hypotheses. Unconfirmed items are listed in "Unknowns and Further Investigation."



ID
Technique
Confidence
Basis




T1611
Escape to Host
high
Corresponds to the public demonstration leading from researcher-owned virtualization environments to host root execution. Production host code execution and third-party attack campaigns remain unconfirmed. Research, Definition




Detailed allocation control leading to host writes and code execution, and applicability conditions for each hypervisor, are not clarified in Part 1.
Reachability across all other virtualization products and configurations, leakage of specific customer data, and actual exploitation by malicious third parties are not substantiated by verified primary sources.
Patch package availability and deployment status across distributions and managed services require individual verification.
The official publication date and time for the primary source are not set. The publication date of October 15, 2026, is estimated from the article record creation date. Update dates can be confirmed in the original metadata.
In AI agent infrastructure, CI systems, and development sandboxes running untrusted code, adopting VMs does not mean the host attack surface has been reduced. In this incident, information accompanying guest communications influenced host kernel write positions and crossed isolation boundaries. In operations, it is crucial not only to manage guest update rates but also to track the application of host kernel patches, and to determine which guests and hosts can be linked to failures or suspicious transmissions. Distinguishing between memory leaks confirmed by providers in production and code execution in research environments helps maintain appropriate urgency without overestimating damage.
For SOCs: Do not judge communication anomalies or host crashes alone as VM escapes; cross-reference guest/host placement information, transmitted packets, and host-side execution evidence.
For Administrators: Verify that the host kernel is patched and that the patched kernel is actually running. Distinguish between stable patch levels and distribution backports/availability.
For Users: Managed sandbox users should check provider response status. Updating within guests alone does not verify host-side remediation.

articles.title: Drupal CVE-2026-108097 and CVE-2026-108099: Pre-Authentication RCE Vectors in Field UI and Entity List
articles.description:
1. Overview




Article Name: Drupal core - Critical - Remote code execution - SA-CORE-2026-014
Source: Drupal Security Team
Publication Date: 2026-10-14
Updated: None
Original: Drupal core Advisory SA-CORE-2026-014


Related Sources: Drupal Entity List Advisory SA-CONTRIB-2026-218, BleepingComputer: Drupal patches critical RCE flaws, warns exploits may emerge soon


Related Malware: None
Related Threat Groups: None
Related CVEs: CVE-2026-108097, CVE-2026-108099
Affected Products: Drupal core Field UI, Drupal Entity List
Severity: High
The Drupal Security Team rated both issues as Critical (19/25) and confirmed known pre-authentication vectors. The core issue is not directly exploitable with Drupal core alone, and the Entity List issue is not directly exploitable with Entity List alone. The reviewed sources do not report exploitation in the wild or a successful public PoC.
Remote code execution vulnerabilities exist in the Drupal core Field UI module and the Entity List contributed module. When combined with other modules or custom code, at least one pre-authentication vector exists. Exploitation in the wild has not been confirmed in the reviewed sources.
The public advisory does not disclose specific module combinations or HTTP requests. The following outlines only the confirmed prerequisite conditions and does not speculate on undisclosed exploits.



Vulnerability ID
Target Component and Scope
Prerequisite Conditions for Exploitation
Updates and Mitigations




CVE-2026-108097
Drupal core Field UI (>= 8.9.0 and < 10.6.19; >= 11.0.0 and < 11.3.19; >= 11.4.0 and < 11.4.10; or >= 12.0.0-alpha1 and < 12.0.0-beta2)
Not directly exploitable in core alone. Requires a combination with a contributed module or custom code (at least one pre-authentication vector confirmed)
Update to supported branches 10.6.19, 11.3.19, 11.4.10, or later (Drupal 12 development branch updates to 12.0.0-beta2 or later). As a temporary workaround, uninstalling Field UI is effective (Drupal Steward protects against only some known vectors)


CVE-2026-108099
Contributed module Entity List (prior to 3.0.10)
Not directly exploitable on its own. Requires a combination with other contributed modules or custom code (at least one pre-authentication vector confirmed)
Update to Entity List 3.0.10 or later. Uninstalling Field UI is a core-side workaround. Drupal Steward protection for this CVE has not been confirmed, and neither serves as a replacement for updating Entity List




An attacker sends a crafted request to an input vector on a publicly accessible Drupal site.
Vulnerable functionality in Field UI or Entity List becomes reachable through another contributed module or custom code.
At least one known vector reaches the processing logic without authentication.
When conditions are met, arbitrary code is executed on the Drupal site server.
Specific module combinations and HTTP request formats are not disclosed in the public advisory.
An external remote attacker who can reach the vulnerable functionality. At least one known vector does not require authentication.
Upon success, code may execute with the process privileges of the web server running Drupal.
Victims and Users: Inference: Users may not notice any anomalies through requests that appear to be normal web browsing.
Administrators: Inference: Indicators may appear as anomalous requests in WAF or web access logs, shell or script execution originating from web processes, unexpected file creation, or unexpected outbound communication. These are not traces actually observed in this incident.
An affected version of Drupal core Field UI or Entity List is running.
Another contributed module or custom code makes the vulnerable functionality reachable from attacker input.
The path is not blocked by patches or mitigations. Uninstalling Field UI is a temporary mitigation for CVE-2026-108097. Protection via Drupal Steward is limited to specific known vectors for that CVE and does not guarantee protection for all vectors or the Entity List side.
Update Drupal core to patched versions 10.6.19, 11.3.19, 11.4.10, or later depending on the supported branch, and update Entity List to 3.0.10 or later. Because Drupal 8/9, 10.5.x and earlier, and 11.2.x and earlier are end-of-life, migrate to a supported branch. The affected range for the Drupal 12 development branch is >= 12.0.0-alpha1 and < 12.0.0-beta2.
If core cannot be updated immediately, uninstall the Field UI module.
Disable unnecessary contributed modules and verify that custom code does not expose Field UI or Entity List functionality to external input.
Arbitrary code executes on the server running Drupal.
Successful execution may lead to web shell deployment, configuration or content tampering, credential access, or execution of additional payloads. However, these follow-on activities have not been confirmed in the wild for these vulnerabilities.
Specific exploit requests are not publicly available. Potential behaviors are evaluated by combining available indicators.
Email: There is no email vector specific to this issue.
Proxy / SWG / DNS: Inference: Review for unusual web requests to the public Drupal site, an increase in errors, and new outbound communication from the server. Specific request formats and module combinations have not been disclosed, so do not limit the investigation to POST or AJAX requests. The scope of visibility depends on log collection settings and retention.
Endpoint / EDR: Inference: Check for shells, script interpreters, or tools like curl or wget spawned by web server or PHP processes, along with the creation of unknown files in the web root or temporary directories.
Identity / IdP: Inference: Check for usage from unknown sources by Drupal administrators or service accounts, though IdP logs may not be generated for known pre-authentication vectors.
SaaS / Cloud: Inference: In managed Drupal or hosting environments, check deployment histories, module versions, WAF configurations, file integrity monitoring (FIM), and container recreation histories.
Network: Inference: Check for unusual outbound connections from the web server, internal reconnaissance, and communication to administrative ports.
Reviewed advisories indicate prerequisite conditions but do not report active exploitation attempts or successful compromises in the wild.
Attack Attempt Observed (Success Unconfirmed): Criteria applied when requests are confirmed to target vulnerable functionality. This does not mean such requests have been observed in public information. Do not judge code execution as successful based solely on suspicious web requests; correlate them with web process execution records, unknown files, and outbound communication.
Scope: Criteria for internal organization investigations. This does not represent public observation records.
Distinguish between RCE preconditions described in research and advisories and actual attack success in real environments.
Investigation Starting Point: Start from the use of affected versions of Field UI / Entity List, unapplied updates, anomalous requests to public Drupal instances, and suspicious web process execution.
Initial Verification: Check versions and enablement states of Drupal core, Entity List, and all contributed modules, alongside custom code, external exposure scope, and update timestamps.
Endpoint and Server Investigation: Preserve changes to the web root, temporary directories, settings.php, module directories, process trees, cron jobs, services, and container images.
Authentication and Cloud Investigation: Review usage history for Drupal administrators, databases, hosting, and cloud credentials to distinguish intrusion via pre-authentication vectors from administrator credential abuse.
Subsequent Activity: Check for web shells, additional users, configuration tampering, database access, internal reconnaissance, and external transmission. These are not confirmed subsequent activities from this incident.
Containment: Inference: Restrict or isolate external access to the target site at the network layer before applying updates. Do not assume that switching to maintenance mode blocks all exploitation vectors. If signs of compromise are present, rebuild from a known good image and rotate related credentials.
Judgment Categories: Evaluate vulnerable configuration presence, attack requests, code execution, persistence, information access, and external transmission separately.
Single Event: Treat the spawning of a shell or script interpreter from a Drupal web process as a high-priority alert.
Temporal Correlation: Correlate anomalous web requests, child process spawning by PHP/web processes, file creation, and outbound communication within a short time window.
Threat Hunting: Cross-check the presence of affected core versions, Entity List prior to 3.0.10, enabled Field UI states, related custom code, and new PHP or script files in the web root.
Log Limitations: Because specific exploit requests and module combinations are private, detection cannot rely solely on IOC matching. Combine process, file, and network telemetry.
Priority Mitigations: Prioritize emergency updates, removal of unnecessary modules, web process execution control, file integrity monitoring, and WAF and outbound traffic control.
CVE-2026-108097 is an RCE vulnerability in the Drupal core Field UI module, which cannot be exploited directly via Drupal core alone.
CVE-2026-108097 has multiple severe exploitation vectors involving combinations with contributed modules, and at least one does not require authentication. Custom code may also expose the vulnerable functionality.
The affected Drupal ranges are >= 8.9.0 and < 10.6.19; >= 11.0.0 and < 11.3.19; >= 11.4.0 and < 11.4.10; or >= 12.0.0-alpha1 and < 12.0.0-beta2.
CVE-2026-108099 is an RCE vulnerability in Entity List prior to 3.0.10, which is not directly exploitable on its own but has at least one pre-authentication vector when combined with other contributed modules or custom code.
Patched versions for supported Drupal core branches are 10.6.19, 11.3.19, 11.4.10, and for Entity List, version 3.0.10. Uninstalling Field UI is a temporary mitigation for CVE-2026-108097 and does not replace fixes on the Entity List side. End-of-life branches require migration to supported branches.
The Drupal Security Team rated both issues as Critical (19/25) with theoretical exploitation, and the reviewed public advisories do not report confirmed exploitation in the wild.
Whether individual Drupal sites are exploitable depends on whether installed contributed modules and custom code connect the vulnerable functionality to external input.
While attack details remain limited, organizations must audit not only updates but also the enablement status of Field UI / Entity List and input paths in surrounding modules on a component basis.
No additional hypotheses. Unverified items are listed under "Unresolved Items and Further Investigation".



ID
Technique
Confidence
Basis




T1190
Exploit Public-Facing Application
medium
Known vectors, including unauthenticated ones, can lead to RCE via module combinations on publicly accessible Drupal sites. Active exploitation is unconfirmed. Source




Specific contributed module combinations, HTTP requests, internal functions, and public PoCs that establish pre-authentication vectors are not disclosed in the advisory.
Scans, attack attempts, and successful compromises in the wild have not been confirmed in public information.
The breakdown of known vectors protected by Drupal Steward and all unprotected vectors has not been published.
Drupal is used in public-facing websites, including government agencies, universities, and non-profit organizations. Organizations should inventory core versions alongside Field UI, Entity List, related contributed modules, and custom code simultaneously. Even after updating, look for suspicious child processes or unexpected file creation by web processes.
For SOCs: Correlate anomalous requests to public Drupal instances with shell or script execution, unknown file creation, and outbound communication originating from web processes.
For Administrators: Update Drupal core to a patched release for the branch you run, and update Entity List to 3.0.10 or later. If core cannot be updated immediately, uninstall Field UI. Do not confuse this temporary mitigation with fixes on the Entity List side.
For Users: This is a server-side vulnerability that does not require user interaction. No special action is required by general users.

articles.title: ConnectWise Cloud Backup Breach: Stolen App Credentials Used to Compromise Microsoft 365 Tenants
articles.description:
1. Basic Information




Article Title: Cloud Backup (formerly known as SkyKick) Service Interruption
Publisher: ConnectWise
Publication Date: 2026-10-16
Updated: 2026-10-18 01:00 UTC
Source: ConnectWise Trust Center


Related Sources: Huntress: ConnectWise (SkyKick) Vendor Credentials Abused in M365 Attacks, Todyl: Unauthorized Access Through the ConnectWise Cloud Backup Microsoft 365 App, BleepingComputer: Hackers breach Microsoft 365 tenants via ConnectWise supply-chain attack, Microsoft: Microsoft Graph activity logs, Microsoft: App Instance Property Lock, Microsoft: Conditional Access for workload identities


Related Malware: None
Related Threat Actor: Unattributed
Related CVE: None
Related Products: ConnectWise Cloud Backup, SkyKick Backup, ConnectWise Cloud Management, Microsoft Entra ID, Microsoft 365, Microsoft Graph
Severity: Critical
Credentials for a multi-tenant application with broad Microsoft Graph permissions were compromised, and Huntress confirmed unauthorized authentication across 162 tenants. In one thoroughly investigated tenant, Global Administrator assignment and persistence via additional credentials were established.
ConnectWise Cloud Backup app credentials were abused to gain unauthorized access to Microsoft 365 through app-only authentication, which does not involve a user sign-in or user MFA. In at least one tenant, the Cloud Management - MS Teams app assigned itself Global Administrator and added client secrets to other apps.
Cloud Backup mass authentication and the privilege escalation and persistence observed by Huntress in a single tenant are organized as independent observations. The latter occurred between 2026-10-15 03:44 and 03:49 UTC, prior to the mass authentication window (06:13 to 08:34 UTC on the same day). It has not been confirmed as part of the same operator's actions, nor does it indicate that privilege escalation or persistence occurred across all tenants.



Category
Observation Time Window (UTC)
Abused Application
Confirmed Activity and Scope




Attack Path A
2026-10-15 06:13 - 08:34
ConnectWise Cloud Backup (formerly SkyKick)
App-only authentication using the OAuth 2.0 client credentials flow and acquisition of tokens for Microsoft Graph. Todyl found no evidence of bulk copying in the tenants it investigated


Attack Path B
2026-10-15 03:44 - 03:49 (Role assignment and credential addition)
ConnectWise Cloud Management - MS Teams
Assignment of Global Administrator to itself and addition of new client secrets to the MSP management app and Huntress app. Seven subsequent sign-ins using the added Huntress credentials were also verified (in the thoroughly investigated tenant)



The scale and aggregation timing of each observation are distinguished in Section 9. Approximately 1,000 tenants and over 300 successful sign-in records associated with the IP address linked to unauthorized activity should not be treated as results confined to this table's Cloud Backup time window.
An attacker obtains vendor-managed Cloud Backup app credentials. The exact leakage vector remains unconfirmed.
The attacker uses the OAuth 2.0 client credentials flow to authenticate to Microsoft Entra ID as an application within the target tenant.
Entra ID issues an app-only access token for Microsoft Graph. No user signs in during this flow, so user MFA does not apply.
The attacker automates this process across target tenants, using the permissions already consented to the Cloud Backup app for email, OneDrive, SharePoint, Teams, and other services.
In the tenants investigated by Todyl, no evidence supporting bulk data copying was found. However, due to audit log limitations, the absence of records does not rule out data access.
The ConnectWise Cloud Management - MS Teams app adds itself to the Global Administrator role.
The same app adds new client secrets to the MSP management app and the Huntress app.
The added Huntress app credentials are used for seven sign-ins within a short timeframe.
Even if the original app is disabled, credentials added to other apps remain valid, requiring individual deletion.
External attackers who possess vendor-managed multi-tenant app credentials and perform app-only authentication to Microsoft 365 from the internet.
Operations in the separately verified tenant utilized Microsoft Graph, Entra app management capabilities, and directory roles. The chronological progression from Cloud Backup mass authentication to this activity has not been confirmed.
Victims and Users: Since standard user logins or MFA prompts do not occur, end users may notice no anomalies.
Administrators: Appears in logs as service principal sign-ins, suspicious IPv4 addresses or Python user-agents associated with Cloud Backup/SkyKick apps, directory role assignments, and added client secrets to existing applications.
ConnectWise Cloud Backup or related Cloud Management applications must be consented and registered in the target tenant.
The attacker must be able to use valid vendor-managed client secrets or certificates.
Data operations require specific Microsoft Graph permissions granted to the target app, while role assignments and credential additions to other apps require separate respective administrative privileges. Successful authentication alone does not imply that these subsequent operations succeeded.
ConnectWise disabled the seven affected application identities at 07:00 UTC on 2026-10-17. Customers should also verify the status of each enterprise application using the official Application ID list and maintain the disabled state until official recovery instructions are released. Vendor-side measures alone do not imply that local settings across all customer tenants changed.
Minimize permissions granted to apps and disable unused old SkyKick/ConnectWise apps.
Audit and delete improperly added client secrets and certificates across all applications. Disabling an app stops the issuance of new tokens, but previously issued tokens may remain usable until expiration. Furthermore, revoking user sessions alone does not stop app-only access.
Within the scope of permissions actually granted to each app, read and write access to emails, attachments, OneDrive/SharePoint files, Teams chats, and directory data may be abused.
Persistence is established through Global Administrator assignment and credential additions to other apps, potentially expanding the impact through the MSP channel.
While Cloud Backup is suspended, new backups and restoration capabilities are interrupted.
The following items are candidates for investigation within your organization. Availability depends on licenses, log settings, and retention periods.
Email: This is not an attack originating from user emails. Check Exchange audit logs for mailbox access by the target Application ID, though identifying the source IP may require additional logs.
Proxy / SWG / DNS: Inference: Authentication requests sent from outside the organization to Microsoft 365 may not traverse the customer's proxy, SWG, or DNS infrastructure. Authentication source IPs and user-agents should be investigated primarily via Entra records.
Endpoint / EDR: Inference: The primary activity environment for this incident is Microsoft 365. Related credentials and scripts on MSP management infrastructure or automation endpoints are supplementary investigation targets, and do not mean that those endpoints themselves were confirmed to be compromised.
Identity / IdP: Search service principal sign-ins for Application IDs 506e08f9-6e9a-4da4-942b-a099a03644ae, 24205314-2b89-4e07-a2a4-579e898a5640, and related IDs from the official list. Verify source IP 144.172.64[.]128, user-agents Python-urllib/3.12 and python-requests/2.31 if recorded, and authentication results. Do not confirm a compromise based solely on IP addresses or user-agents, and do not rule out Azure-internal sources.
SaaS / Cloud: Investigate role assignments and credential additions using Entra audit logs, and check operations on email, files, and Teams using available Unified Audit Logs. Pre-collected MicrosoftGraphActivityLogs are records for examining Graph API requests and sources, which are distinct from token issuance events themselves. Full visibility of read activities may not always be available.
Network: Inference: Standard customer network logs may not capture external authentication to Microsoft 365 or Graph API usage. Correlate Entra authentication records and collected Graph API requests using app IDs, timestamps, sources, and available correlation IDs.
Malware Execution or Successful Authentication Confirmed: Huntress confirmed unauthorized app authentication across 162 tenants as of 2026-10-16 19:00 UTC. The 2026-10-17 update confirmed activity across approximately 1,000 tenants and over 300 successful sign-in records associated with the IP address linked to unauthorized activity, but the latter does not imply an equivalent number of compromised tenants. Data exfiltration remains unconfirmed.
Scope: Microsoft 365 authentication for ConnectWise Cloud Backup / related apps
Subsequent Compromise Confirmed: In one tenant, the Cloud Management - MS Teams app acquired Global Administrator privileges and added client secrets to two other apps, with the added Huntress credentials used for seven sign-ins. Data reading has not been confirmed.
Scope: One customer tenant thoroughly investigated by Huntress
Separate authentication success, data access, privilege escalation, and persistence stage by stage, and do not treat successful sign-in counts directly as the number of compromised tenants.
Investigation Starting Point: Start with the usage status of ConnectWise Cloud Backup/SkyKick, sign-ins for target Application IDs, suspicious IPs, Python user-agents, and app credential changes.
Initial Review: Verify across all tenants whether target apps exist, their enabled status, granted permissions, directory roles, and service principal sign-ins since October 13.
Endpoint and Server Investigation: Check whether client secrets or certificates for target apps are stored or used on MSP management infrastructure or automation endpoints, and preserve related scripts and credentials.
Authentication and Cloud Investigation: Check Entra audit logs for role assignments, OAuth consent, and service principal credential additions, and trace API-level sources using MicrosoftGraphActivityLogs if available.
Subsequent Operations: Investigate sign-ins by other apps holding added client secrets, reading of emails, files, and Teams, and MSP cross-tenant access.
Containment: Disable rather than delete target apps, and remove unauthorized client secrets, certificates, and roles. Verify the validity period of issued tokens and access paths remaining in other apps, and continue monitoring until recovery instructions are released. Revoking user sessions does not replace invalidating app-only tokens.
Decision Categories: Evaluate authentication attempts, app-only token issuance, data access, role assignments, added credentials, and re-authentication in separate apps independently.
Single Event: Treat the assignment of Global Administrator to a high-privilege service principal or the addition of new client secrets to existing security/MSP apps as high-priority alerts.
Chronological Correlation: Correlate role assignment within a tenant -> credential addition to another app -> sign-in using the added credentials. Investigate Cloud Backup mass authentication and subsequent API requests separately, avoiding unverified chronological connections between the two observations.
Threat Hunting: Audit all tenants for ConnectWise publisher apps including legacy SkyKick, excessive Graph permissions, and client secrets or certificates added since October 13, 2026.
Log Limitations: Standard Entra audit logs alone cannot identify sources of Graph reads by apps, and MicrosoftGraphActivityLogs cannot be retrieved retroactively prior to enablement. For periods without collection, data access scope may remain undetermined.
Priority Mitigations: Prioritize least-privilege principles for service principals, immediate detection of app credential changes, and log preservation. Since App Instance Property Lock is a mechanism configured on the publisher side managing app registrations, verify implementation status with providers for third-party apps. Furthermore, user-focused Conditional Access does not protect this app-only flow. Conditional Access for workload identities does not cover third-party multitenant apps, so it should not be treated as a way to block these affected applications.
ConnectWise confirmed unauthorized access to application IDs related to Cloud Backup, revoked certificates for affected connections across all users, and invalidated shared credentials.
Huntress confirmed unauthorized sign-ins across 162 tenants as of 2026-10-16 19:00 UTC. The 2026-10-17 update confirmed sign-in activity spanning approximately 1,000 tenants with over 300 successful records, but this aggregation is not a confirmed count of 300 compromised tenants.
Attackers authenticated as the Cloud Backup app using the OAuth 2.0 client credentials flow, obtaining Microsoft Graph app-only tokens without user login.
Due to existing consent granted to the Cloud Backup app, read/write and restoration capabilities for email, attachments, OneDrive, SharePoint, and Teams chats were available. In the tenants investigated by Todyl, no evidence supporting bulk data copying was found.
In one tenant examined in detail by Huntress, the Cloud Management - MS Teams app assigned Global Administrator to itself and added new client secrets to the MSP management app and Huntress app. The added Huntress credentials were used for seven sign-ins.
ConnectWise stated that there is no evidence of access to encrypted backup archives. Meanwhile, since the company cannot directly inspect downstream Microsoft 365 environments, customers must investigate app activity on their own.
In its update on 2026-10-18 01:00 UTC, ConnectWise explained that it disabled the seven affected application identities at 07:00 UTC the previous day, and that issued tokens or changes to other IDs require additional actions. Cloud Backup remains suspended with restoration timing undetermined. The statement that no successful threat activity was observed after mitigation applies only to ConnectWise's monitoring scope.
Because app-only authentication does not involve a user sign-in, user MFA and user-focused Conditional Access do not protect this flow. Service principal credentials and permissions therefore need to be monitored as high-value identities in their own right.
Since some Graph reads cannot be isolated to their sources using standard audit logs alone, organizations that have not pre-collected MicrosoftGraphActivityLogs may be unable to determine the full scope of data access.
No additional hypotheses. Unconfirmed items are listed in "Unknowns and Additional Investigation".



ID
Technique
Confidence
Basis




T1078.004
Valid Accounts: Cloud Accounts
high
Authenticated to Microsoft 365 tenants via app-only using compromised vendor-managed app credentials. Source



T1098.001
Account Manipulation: Additional Cloud Credentials
high
Added new client secrets to an existing MSP management application and the Huntress application in one tenant. Source




The specific vector by which app credentials leaked on the ConnectWise side, the threat actor's identity, and the total number of impacted tenants remain unconfirmed.
The actual scope of exfiltrated email, file, and Teams data has not been verified. Due to audit log limitations, the absence of records does not rule out access.
Whether role assignments by Cloud Management apps constituted legitimate vendor processing has not been confirmed for all tenants. It is also unconfirmed whether the credential addition in one tenant and the Cloud Backup mass authentication were performed by the same operator.
MSPs and SaaS backups represent a highly concentrated trust boundary where a single set of app credentials can reach numerous customer tenants. Organizations should verify across all tenants whether Cloud Backup (formerly SkyKick) is deployed, and prioritize investigating service principal sign-ins, app credential changes, directory role assignments, and Graph activity rather than user sign-ins.
For SOCs: Search service principal sign-ins for suspicious IPs, Python user-agents, and target Application IDs, and correlate role assignments with added credentials chronologically.
For Administrators: Disable target apps according to ConnectWise instructions without deleting them, and review client secrets, certificates, and directory roles across all applications.
For Users: This is a cloud-side compromise occurring without user MFA interaction. User re-authentication or session revocation alone cannot stop app access, requiring administrative handling of apps and credentials.

articles.title: The hundredth clip costs nothing: Klipkit, a local-first clip finder for freelance editors
articles.description:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 2: Side Hustle
Klipkit is a clip finder for freelance short-form editors that runs entirely on a laptop — no upload, no per-minute API bill, no NDA problem.
Point it at a podcast, a stream VOD or a client's raw footage. It transcribes the audio locally, finds the moments that work as standalone clips, writes a hook line for each, and exports a client-ready pack: MP4 + .srt + a run sheet with timecodes.
source ──► whisper (local) ──► candidate moments ──► local LLM judge ──► clip pack
file/URL     word timestamps     cheap heuristics      open-weight model     mp4 + srt

Who would pay for it: freelance clippers and short-form editors who get paid per clip and work under NDA. They have two problems that hosted tools make worse.
Per-minute pricing: cloud clip tools charge by upload-minute. If a client sends a two-hour podcast and you pull eight clips, you pay for the whole two hours. Do that for ten clients and the tooling costs more than the job.
And the footage isn't theirs. Clients send raw footage under NDA — uploading it to a server the client doesn't control is a non-starter, and "we have a SOC 2 report" is not a satisfying answer when the contract says the file never leaves the editor's machine.
So the business only works if the marginal cost of the hundredth clip is zero. That requires local inference, which requires open weights.
No hosted link, and that's the point — Klipkit runs locally, so there is nothing to deploy. Here is a real run on a public 62-minute Indonesian-language talk video, on an RTX 2050 with 4 GB of VRAM:
$ klipkit run "https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=zOnA_8JmdM8" -n 5 --whisper small --llm gemma3:1b

  Top moments - NEPHILIM, NABI ADAM & RAKSASA PURBA...

│ 2 │ 00:03:37 │ 00:04:23 │ 46s │  0.91 │ -    │
│ 3 │ 00:14:16 │ 00:15:05 │ 49s │  0.91 │ -    │

Test source is a public YouTube video, used only as input. Klipkit processed it locally — nothing was re-uploaded, and the rendered clips stay on my machine.



Stage
Result




Transcribe
9,612 words, language id at 0.99 confidence, ~6 min on GPU

Roughly ten minutes of wall clock, six of it transcription. The SRT timings come out of the same word timings used for cutting, so captions stay locked to the audio instead of drifting.
The empty Hook column is the honest part of this demo, and I get into it below.
 / 
        klipkit
      
    

Klipkit
Find the clips worth posting — on your own laptop, with no cloud in the loop.
Klipkit is a local-first clip finder built for freelance clippers and short-form video editors

and exports a client-ready pack (MP4 + .srt captions + a notes sheet).
Nothing leaves your machine. No upload, no per-minute API bill, no NDA problem.
                                                    
  source ──► whisper (local) ──► candidate moments ──► local LLM judge ──► clip pack
  file/URL     word timestamps     cheap heuristics      open-weight model     mp4 + srt



Why local, and why open
Freelance clippers are paid per clip, so two things kill their margin: time and API cost
Cloud clip tools charge per upload-minute, which makes high-volume work unprofitable, and they…

  
View on GitHub
MIT licensed. Python, with faster-whisper, Ollama, ffmpeg and yt-dlp as the only real dependencies.
The open-source AI is the product, not a decoration. Four open pieces do all the work:



Piece
Role
Why it has to be open




faster-whisper
transcription with word-level timestamps
runs offline, no per-minute fee, audio never leaves the disk


Ollama + Gemma 3
judges which moments are clip-worthy, writes the hooks
runs on a laptop GPU, swappable, free forever


ffmpeg
cutting and caption rendering
already on every editor's machine


yt-dlp
optional URL import
no vendor gatekeeping your sources



The design decision that mattered most: the model never sees the whole transcript.
An hour of talk audio is ~10,000 words. Feeding that to a small open-weight model in one shot produces garbage — it loses the thread and burns context on filler. So the pipeline layers cheap and expensive. Heuristics run first and cost nothing: overlapping 45-second windows are scored on question openers, digits, filler density, and whether the cut starts mid-thought. Only the top slice reaches the model.
# klipkit/text.py
def rank_candidates(candidates, keep_ratio=0.5, min_keep=8, max_keep=16):
    ranked = sorted(candidates, key=lambda c: c.heuristic, reverse=True)
    keep = max(min_keep, int(len(candidates) * keep_ratio))
    keep = min(keep, max_keep, len(ranked))
    return sorted(ranked[:keep], key=lambda c: c.start)

That cap does real work: 606 candidates became 16, which is four small batches of judging instead of 606. Ollama runs the judge with format: "json" so the model is constrained to a parseable reply, and the whole pipeline ran on a 4 GB laptop GPU.
What broke on the way — the parts I'd want to read before trying this myself:
1. yt-dlp now requires a JavaScript runtime. Since the 2026 releases, YouTube extraction needs one, and it degrades with a vague "some formats may be missing" warning instead of an error. Node was already installed; the Python API just wasn't being told about it.
# klipkit/ingest.py
opts = {
    "format": "bv*[height<=720][ext=mp4]+ba[ext=m4a]/b[height<=720]/bv*[height<=720]+ba/b",
    "js_runtimes": {"node": {}},   # without this, YouTube extraction silently degrades
}

2. av 19 broke faster-whisper. Not a warning — a hard crash on every input, because av.open() gained a metadata_errors keyword that faster-whisper 1.2.1 doesn't pass. The fix belongs in pyproject.toml, not a README footnote:
dependencies = [
    "faster-whisper>=1.1",
    "av<15",
    "yt-dlp>=2025.1.1",
]

3. cuBLAS wasn't on LD_LIBRARY_PATH. faster-whisper picked CUDA via device="auto", model construction succeeded, then encoding failed with Library libcublas.so.12 is not found. The library existed — bundled inside Ollama's own runtime. Pointing LD_LIBRARY_PATH at it took the GPU to 98% utilization. Worth knowing before concluding your GPU is unsupported.
4. Gemma 3 1b is too small to batch-score reliably. This is the empty Hook column. I asked it to score four candidates at once and return JSON; it returned verdicts for one or two, and one batch came back as an HTTP 500 from Ollama. Every clip fell back to heuristic scoring.
That's a model-capability limit, not a pipeline bug. The default is gemma3:4b for a reason — I only had the 1b because the Ollama registry was unreachable from this machine and I imported the GGUF from HuggingFace directly. It's also the clearest argument for the swappable-model design: the fix is a flag, not a rewrite.
Three things about this project only exist because the pieces are open.
The marginal cost is actually zero. A closed API that charges per minute makes high-volume freelance work unprofitable. Running Gemma 3 locally means the hundredth clip costs the same as the first: nothing. That isn't a discount, it's the difference between a tool a freelancer can build a business on and a tool that eats their margin.
The client's footage never leaves the laptop. This is a hard requirement, not a preference. No closed API can satisfy an NDA clause that says the file stays on the editor's machine — no matter how good its privacy policy is. Local open-weight inference is the only architecture that makes the promise structurally true instead of contractually promised.
I can swap the brain without touching the pipeline. --llm gemma3:1b for a fast pass, gemma3:4b when a clip really matters, or something else entirely next month. When I discovered the 1b model couldn't batch-score, the fix was one flag. With a hosted API, model quality is a vendor decision I'd have to wait on.
The open pieces are also what let a 1b model and a 4 GB GPU be enough. I'm not paying per token, so layering a free heuristic prefilter in front of an expensive judge is pure upside — 606 candidates down to 16 before the model sees anything.
Best Use of Gemma — Gemma 3 is the judge at the centre of the pipeline, not a bolt-on. It scores hook strength, self-containment, payoff and energy for each shortlisted moment and writes the on-screen hook line. The project ships with gemma3:4b as the default and treats the model as swappable, so the same code runs a 1b or a larger Gemma depending on the hardware and how much the clip matters.
The local-LLM stack I leaned on is well-trodden on DEV, and these shaped how I built it:
Build a Voice-Controlled Local AI Agent with Ollama and Faster-Whisper by Shaik Idris — the Whisper + Ollama pairing that made this feel buildable on a laptop.
Local Meeting Notes with Whisper Transcription + Ollama Summaries (Gemma3n, LLaMA, Mistral) — Meetily AI by Zackriya — proof that local transcription plus a local summarizer is a real product shape, not a demo.
Clean JSON Extraction with Ollama and Python by nearshi — the parsing discipline I should have applied before discovering the 1b model's partial responses the hard way.
Taming Local LLM Non-Determinism: Building a Resilient, Multi-Stage JSON Sanitizer & Schema Adapter in Python by toai — the repair-validate-retry pattern that's now first on my list.
Score one candidate at a time and accept the latency. Batching looked like an obvious token saving, but a 1b model can't hold four scoring rubrics in its head at once, and a partial JSON response is worse than a slow complete one — the fallback silently degrades quality instead of failing loudly.
Make the fallback visible. "scored by heuristics only" is currently a note in the run sheet. It should be a warning at the top, because a pack with five empty hook columns looks like a working result.
Test on a short source first. My first real test was 62 minutes, so every iteration cost six minutes of transcription. A three-minute clip would have caught the av crash in seconds.
Talk-heavy footage is where this shines. B-roll-driven video has no transcript worth judging.
Auto-reframing to 9:16 is deliberately not in v1 — a bad vertical crop is worse than none. Klipkit hands the editor timecodes and captions and lets them reframe in CapCut.
Non-Latin scripts and heavy code-switching depend on Whisper's coverage.
No first user yet. The next step is handing it to an editor with a real client backlog and watching which flag they reach for first.
Run it yourself: klipkit doctor tells you what's missing before you spend six minutes finding out.

articles.title: Woolly: Gemma proposes the tasks. Only the client can pay for them.
articles.description:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 2: Side Hustle
Woolly is a board for a client who pays a few freelancers against a project budget.
The client sets the budget, then puts an allocation on each cycle. Tasks on that project split the allocated money, and the shares always add up to 100%. A worker can edit a task and submit proof. Marking it complete requires a written summary of the proof, and that moves the task to Under Review. The client is the only person who can approve it (Complete) or send it back (Revision Needed). A worker who tries to approve their own work is refused by the server.
That is the thing someone would pay for. A client who already hires people by the piece wants the money to stay a percentage of a number they typed, with one approver. Woolly is not a marketplace and it does not send invoices. It is the agreement: budget, cycles, shares, proof, and a client who decides.
In the walkthrough, Field notes has an $800 allocation and four tasks. Each one sits at 25%, $200. Move one slider and the others give up the remainder so the total stays 100%.
Gemma does not touch that number. A client can paste a summary ("add the landing page to Cycle 1") and a Mastra agent asks Gemma to propose the tasks, on the cycle named in the summary. If that cycle is missing, the task comes back unplaced. The agent does not quietly pick a different cycle. A second agent can recommend credit or dispute on a proof. The recommendation is stored. The payment decision is a separate action, and only the client can take it.
The people in the demo are fictional: Cool Client, Worker One, and Worker Dos. There is no password.
  
  


The video is the client board, a task and its allocation, Manage (budgets and cycles), a new project, then the same app as Worker One. The worker has no project button and no Settings. The account menu is Sign out. Nothing in the recording is saved.
To run it locally, from a clone of the repo:
cd server && npm install && npm run migrate && npm run dev
cd app && flutter run -d chrome

Copy .env.example to .env first. The API listens on http://127.0.0.1:8787, and the app is the Flutter web client. npm run migrate rebuilds the tables and the fictional rows. Sign in as Cool Client or Worker One.
The board loads without a model call. Gemma runs when someone asks for tasks from a summary, or for a recommendation on a proof.
 / 
        woolly
      
    

Woolly
Pay for an iteration, measured by the subtasks a client accepts.
A project is the epic. An iteration is one sprint inside that project: it has an amount and an optional deadline. Tasks are the stories. Subtasks are the tickets. Pay for an iteration is its amount times the share of subtask effort the client has credited.
A client has many workers. A worker has many projects. The client adds work and reviews it, filtered by worker or by project. The worker adds and edits tasks, and submits subtasks for review. The worker cannot credit their own work.
The people in the demo are fictional: Cool Client (client), Worker One (worker), and Worker Dos (worker).
Demo
Walkthrough of the client board, task allocation, Manage, and the worker account: https://youtu.be/IX1FJzK4vcU
Look
Dark brown, flat, closer to a Darcula editor than a paper form. Near-black background, warm brown panels, amber marks…





  
View on GitHub
MIT. github.com/jedau/woolly
The open pieces are Gemma and Mastra. Gemma is gemma-4-26b-a4b-it, called through the Gemini API (server/src/env.ts). It is an open-weight model on a hosted endpoint. This build does not run the weights on the laptop, and I am not going to pretend it does. Proof text and summaries go to that API when an agent runs.
Mastra is the harness (server/src/woolly.ts):



Agent
Job




Place
Turn a summary into one task per piece of work, on the cycle the summary names


Split
Break a brief into tasks and subtasks. Effort is the size, value is how much it matters


Review
Read a proof against the description and recommend credit or dispute



Place and split return JSON the server checks before anything is written. Review writes model_outcome on the proof. The client's decision is a different request. Shares are basis points on the task row, and the server normalizes them so a project sums to 10000. Cycle allocations that would pass the project budget are rejected. None of that is a sentence in the prompt.
search-past-work is a Mastra tool the split and review agents call. It looks up this project's own accepted subtasks, with Postgres full text and a pgvector embedding, and hands a few titles back. The embedding call is Gemini's embedding model, not Gemma. The memory is the client's past work, not a general chat log.
flowchart LR
  summary[Client summary] --> place[Mastra place agent]
  place --> gemma[Gemma via the Gemini API]
  gemma --> tasks[Tasks on the named cycle]
  tasks --> board[Board and allocation]
  proof[Worker proof] --> review[Mastra review agent]
  review --> note[Recommendation only]
  note --> client[Client approves or sends it back]
  client --> paid[Share of the allocation]
Stack around that: a Flutter web client, a TypeScript API, Postgres. The theme is a dark brown board. Projects, workers, cycle, and status are filters. The client and the worker are two workplaces in one app.
A client will pay for this only if the money rule is boring and visible. An allocation is a number they set. A share is a percentage of that number. A worker cannot approve the proof. If those rules lived inside a closed chat product, the same vendor would propose the work and hold the ledger, and a prompt would be the only thing standing between a suggestion and a payment.
Other people building agents next to money are drawing the same line. A spending limit written in a prompt is not a control (Prompts don't enforce budgets. Signatures do.), and the approval has to sit outside the model (Should this AI agent be allowed to pay?). Woolly keeps Gemma on the proposal. The budget check, the shares, and the approver check are ordinary server code.
Open is what makes the split possible. Mastra is the harness, so the three agents are a file I can read, and the model is a setting (GEMINI_MODEL, default gemma-4-26b-a4b-it) rather than the product. I can point Place at another Gemma endpoint without rewriting who is allowed to mark a task paid. The board also has a price of zero when nobody is asking the model anything. The calls a client would pay for are the ones that propose work or read a proof.
What open does not do here: it does not keep the proof on the machine. Hosted Gemma means a summary leaves the laptop when an agent runs. Local weights would close that gap. They are not what this submission runs.
Featured
Best Use of Gemma. Place, split, and review are Gemma (gemma-4-26b-a4b-it through the Gemini API). Place turns a summary into tasks. Review recommends credit or dispute and does not get to apply it.
Partner
Best Use of Mastra. Those three agents are Mastra Agents, and past work is a createTool the split and review agents call before they answer.
Solo entry.
